title: StateGuard denies every build option: minerals_remaining is a shortfall, not a budget
description:
StateGuard treats minerals_remaining as a spendable budget. It is a SHORTFALL. So on any base that has accumulated minerals toward its current item, the guard denies EVERY option and base.production degrades to the deterministic tier - including, and especially, the correct choice.

MEASURED END TO END on a live game, turn 42, Morgan Solutions (Morganites):

  base_state: current Colony Pod, minerals_accumulated 27, cost 33, mineral_surplus 7
  metrics:    minerals_remaining 6
  action_space (every entry): effects {"minerals_remaining": -<full item cost>}
      unit:0   Colony Pod           cost 33  turns_if_switched 5  turns_if_continued 1
      unit:1   Formers              cost 22  turns_if_switched 4
      unit:2   Scout Patrol         cost 11  turns_if_switched 2
      unit:256 Synthmetal Garrison  cost 22  ...  (and four facilities at 44-220)

  agent chose unit:0 - the item already in production, 27/33 banked, ONE TURN from completion
  guard advisory: "unit:0 spends 33 minerals_remaining but only 6 is available - the state moved since this was offered"
  submit result:  degraded=true, degrade_reason="guard denied every choice (1 stripped); 1 repair attempt(s) also failed"
  adapter row:    tier=llm, applied=llm_degraded, applied_item_name=Colony Pod

THE CATEGORY ERROR, from both ends:
  - metrics.py:134-139 defines minerals_remaining as "Minerals still needed to finish what this base is building", direction "lower is better".
  - thinker neural.cpp:559-562 emits it as (total_cost - minerals_accumulated), clamped at 0. A shortfall.
  - thinker neural.cpp:351 declares every action's effects as {"minerals_remaining": -cost}, the FULL item cost.
  - hank.py StateGuard then reads "spends 33, only 6 available" and denies.

Nothing here is a state race, so the advisory's "the state moved since this was offered" is also wrong and actively misleading - it sends the reader looking for a concurrency bug that does not exist.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY FALSE POSITIVE:
  1. It denies the ENTIRE action space, not one option. Every item costs more than the shortfall by construction, because the shortfall is at most the cheapest thing the base is already building. So the LLM tier cannot land ANY choice on a base mid-build.
  2. It is hardest on the decision the project most wants right: continuing a nearly-finished item. 27 banked minerals and turns_if_continued=1 is the textbook continuity case that na-61c.2's history work and the play skill's "prefer continuity" guidance exist to get right - and the guard vetoes exactly that.
  3. It is invisible in aggregate as a QUALITY problem. The game still gets a legal item (the deterministic fallback picked the same Colony Pod here), so nothing looks broken; the run just quietly stops being an LLM-tier run. The decision record does say degraded=true, so it IS measurable - degrade_rate on base.production should be near 1.0 on any developed game, which is the number to check.

CANDIDATE FIXES, and the choice matters:
  (a) Stop declaring item cost against minerals_remaining. An item's cost is not a withdrawal from a shortfall. For a SWITCH the meaningful effect is that the accumulated minerals are forfeited; for CONTINUING it is that the shortfall falls to zero. Both are expressible, neither is "-cost".
  (b) Teach StateGuard that a "lower is better" shortfall metric is not a resource pool and must not be treated as an affordability budget. This is the more general fix - the same trap waits for any future metric with that direction.
  (c) Declare cost against a metric that IS a pool. There is no per-base mineral pool in the vocabulary today (minerals_accumulated is not in metrics.py), which is why (a) was reached for.

(b) plus (a) is the honest pair: the guard should not infer a budget from a direction, and the adapter should not declare an effect it cannot mean.

ACCEPTANCE: on a base with accumulated minerals, an agent choosing the item already in production is APPLIED (adapter row tier=llm, applied=llm, not llm_degraded), and no advisory claims the state moved. Add a regression test with a world view shaped like the one above - banked 27, cost 33, minerals_remaining 6.

Found while running na-1wu. It is the reason base.production has no tier=llm/applied=llm row yet, while faction.se has four.
close_reason: Fix is live and verified three ways: metrics.py Metric.pool + is_pool() present, hank.py:190-198 gates on 'if not is_pool(metric): continue' with a comment naming na-co2, and 52 guard/pool/state tests pass. Close commit 668a08a already recorded a live before/after on identical state (turn 42, Colony Pod 27/33: llm_degraded -> llm, degraded=false). Engineering finished 2026-08-01; the bead has been re-dispatching because status writes to this embedded store are not sticking (aegis-t15jl) — my own defer earlier this session also did not persist.

title: Decision log records tier=llm applied for decisions the game abandoned (llm_timeout_ms=2500)
description:
The orchestrator records tier=llm, degraded=false, "applied to the game" for decisions the game ALREADY ABANDONED. Measured end to end on a live game at turn 39.

WHAT HAPPENED

Ran the agent-brain loop against a real game: NA_BRAIN=agent, orchestrator up, thinker posting to 127.0.0.1:8000. Answered two decisions through /agent/next + /agent/submit. Both returned:

  {"submitted":"unit:0","applied":["unit:0"],"status":"applied to the game","degraded":false}

and the orchestrator's decision log recorded:

  faction.se       t39 Gaians tier=llm degraded=False chosen=['se:none']
  base.production  t39 Hive   tier=llm degraded=False chosen=['unit:0']

The ADAPTER's own log for the same turn says the opposite. Zero rows with tier=llm out of 66; every base.production and faction.se row reads:

  tier=deterministic  applied=native  fallback_reason="orchestrator unreachable or slow"

So the game asked, gave up, applied Thinker's own pick, and moved on. The answer I submitted minutes later was accepted by an orchestrator that had no idea the decision was dead, and written into the record of truth as a successful LLM-tier decision that was applied. It was not applied. Nothing in the decision log distinguishes it from a real one.

ROOT CAUSE, two defects

1. THE TIMEOUT DEFAULT CONTRADICTS ITS OWN DOCUMENTATION.
   thinker src/main.h:180  -> `int llm_timeout_ms = 2500;`
   thinker src/na_http.cpp:285 -> "timeout_ms <= 0 means wait indefinitely, which is the
   configured default."
   Those cannot both be true, and the code wins: the adapter waits 2.5 seconds. thinker.ini
   ships without an llm_timeout_ms line, so 2500 is what every run gets.

   .claude/skills/play-alpha-centauri/SKILL.md tells the agent "The game blocks while you
   think ... there is no clock on your reasoning." That is false against this build by three
   orders of magnitude. An attached agent cannot answer in 2.5s; a human-driven one certainly
   cannot. So on the current default the agent brain CANNOT EVER win the race, and every
   agent-tier run silently degrades to Thinker while reporting success.

2. THE ORCHESTRATOR CANNOT KNOW, AND CLAIMS ANYWAY.
   /agent/submit returns "status":"applied to the game". It has no signal from the adapter that
   the application happened - the adapter already returned native_choice to the engine and hung
   up. A pending decision is never expired, so an answer arriving after the game moved on is
   indistinguishable from one that arrived in time.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN A NORMAL BUG

It corrupts the record of truth in the direction that flatters us. docs/observability.md 5.4
exists to catch "a run of pure fallbacks that completes and looks green". This is that failure
inverted and made invisible: the fallbacks ARE recorded, correctly, in the adapter log - and the
orchestrator writes a second, contradictory record marking them llm-tier successes. Every number
derived from the decision log is affected: coverage, degrade_rate, tier attribution, directive
attention and override rates (na-mmp), and any A/B outcome measurement (na-6db). A measurement
that reads 'the LLM tier decided this' when Thinker decided it cannot be corrected after the
fact, because both records look well-formed.

It also invalidates the obvious reading of na-1wu / na-ckn. Submitting successfully and seeing
tier=llm in the decision log is NOT evidence the loop closed. The only proof is a tier=llm row in
the ADAPTER's na-observations.jsonl, or applied_item matching what the agent chose.

FIX

- Short term, unblocks the P0s: set llm_timeout_ms explicitly. 0 for the documented
  wait-indefinitely behaviour, or a large finite value (300000) so an unanswered decision cannot
  freeze the game forever. Either way thinker.ini must carry the line rather than inherit 2500.
- Reconcile main.h:180 with na_http.cpp:285. One of them is lying and the comment is the one
  people read.
- The orchestrator must stop asserting what it cannot observe. Either expire a pending decision
  once the adapter's deadline has passed and record it as abandoned, or have the adapter confirm
  application and only then finalise the record. "status":"applied to the game" should be
  reported by the side that applied it.
- Correct the SKILL's "no clock on your reasoning" line to state the real bound.

Note there is already a related commit, thinker 267275a "fix(neural): record a cached decision
that the board overtook" - same family (an answer arriving after the world moved), different
path.

VERIFY BY MECHANISM, NOT BY THE REPORTING INTERFACE: two logs disagreed here and the one that
was easy to read was the wrong one.
close_reason: All four of the bead's own fix items verified done in code, not by commit message: (1) llm_timeout_ms now provisioned and brain-coupled (87e3147, mine); (2) main.h/na_http.cpp comment reconciled (692080d) — 2500 correctly retained for non-agent brains; (3) orchestrator stops asserting what it cannot observe (bf3170e) — _accepted_status no longer says 'applied to the game', AgentBrain abandons before the engine via ABANDON_MARGIN_SECONDS, late submits get 409 telling the agent not to resubmit; (4) SKILL.md:12 corrected. Full suite 477 passed 0 failed. Residual late-finish path is now REPORTED as late rather than recorded as an applied llm decision — the silent flattering misrecord this bead was about is gone. Dead-process pendings remain na-bzd.

comments.author: ellie
comments.text:
ADAPTER HALF LANDED — NeuralAmplifier 87e3147. Orchestrator half is NOT done (na-bzd).
(ellie, 2026-08-02)

MEASURED WHAT WAS ACTUALLY LEFT, because two of this bead's four fix items were already done:

  [DONE, 692080d] Reconcile main.h:197 with na_http.cpp:285. The comment now states the truth
                  ("that is the INTENDED default and it is NOT what ships").
  [DONE]          SKILL.md "no clock on your reasoning" — line 12 now reads "but only for
                  llm_timeout_ms, and the built-in default is ...".
  [DONE, 87e3147] thinker.ini must carry the line rather than inherit 2500.  <- this commit
  [NOT DONE]      The orchestrator must stop asserting what it cannot observe.  -> na-bzd

THE GAP WAS NARROWER AND WORSE THAN THE BEAD STATES. The bead says "thinker.ini ships without an
llm_timeout_ms line". True, but the repo's thinker.ini has no llm block AT ALL — play-thinker.sh
WRITES one (llm_factions, llm_endpoint) and omitted llm_timeout_ms. So the provisioner that
exists to configure the gate was the thing that left the timeout inherited. Grepped the whole
tree: before this commit llm_timeout_ms appeared only in docs, comments and tests, and in NO
file the engine reads.

AND 2500 IS NOT ITSELF A BUG — worth stating, because "raise the default" is the obvious wrong
fix. main.h chooses it "to cover a Haiku call on a warm connection", which is right for the LLM
tier and is what keeps a dead orchestrator from hanging a turn (invariant 9). It is wrong only
for the ONE brain invariant 9 already carves an exception for. AGENTS.md:59-66 documents that
exception and says to set "NA_AGENT_TIMEOUT (and llm_timeout_ms on the adapter)" — so this was a
documented requirement that nothing implemented.

FIX: the timeout now follows the brain, which is the coupling AGENTS.md requires.
    NA_LLM_TIMEOUT_MS set -> that value      NA_BRAIN=agent -> 300000      else -> 2500
All three verified, plus idempotence against the real play dir (an ini already carrying
llm_timeout_ms=0 is left alone and the value reported, matching the existing llm_factions rule).
Finite rather than 0 deliberately: <=0 means wait indefinitely, and an unattended run that hangs
forever is what NA_TIMEOUT exists to catch (na-ie9) — under Xvfb a hung game looks exactly like
a working one.

The script now WARNS when it takes 2500 with no NA_BRAIN set. The silence was the defect.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT FIX, so nobody reads this as closing the P0: the orchestrator still returns
"status":"applied to the game" for something it cannot observe, and a pending decision from a
dead game is still accepted. Until na-bzd lands, the decision log can still record a tier=llm
success for a decision the game abandoned — this commit only stops the agent from LOSING the
race by construction. Leaving na-t3h OPEN for that reason.

VERIFY BY MECHANISM, per this bead's own closing line: the proof an agent decision landed is a
tier=llm row in the ADAPTER's na-observations.jsonl, or applied_item matching what the agent
chose — never the orchestrator's own record.

comments.author: ellie
comments.text:
CLOSING — all four of this bead's own FIX items are done and verified by mechanism.
(ellie, 2026-08-02)

The bead lists four fixes. I checked each against the code rather than against its commit
message, because a commit existing is not the code being live — the lesson na-co2 just taught
me three dispatches running.

  [1] "thinker.ini must carry the line rather than inherit 2500"
      DONE — 87e3147 (mine, this session). The gap was narrower than the bead states: the repo
      thinker.ini has no llm block AT ALL; play-thinker.sh WRITES one (llm_factions,
      llm_endpoint) and omitted the timeout. Grepped the tree first: llm_timeout_ms appeared
      only in docs, comments and tests, never in a file the engine reads.
      The timeout now FOLLOWS THE BRAIN, which is the coupling AGENTS.md:65 already required:
        NA_LLM_TIMEOUT_MS -> that value | NA_BRAIN=agent -> 300000 | else -> 2500
      All three verified, plus idempotence against the real play dir (an ini already carrying
      llm_timeout_ms=0 is left alone). Finite not 0: <=0 is wait-indefinitely and a hung
      unattended run is indistinguishable from a working one under Xvfb (na-ie9).

  [2] "Reconcile main.h:197 with na_http.cpp:285"
      DONE — 692080d. Read the comment: it now states the truth outright ("that is the INTENDED
      default and it is NOT what ships"). main.h still defaults 2500 and that is CORRECT — it is
      chosen "to cover a Haiku call on a warm connection" and is what keeps invariant 9 for
      every non-agent brain. Raising it would have been the obvious wrong fix.

  [3] "The orchestrator must stop asserting what it cannot observe"
      DONE — bf3170e. Verified in code, not just message:
        service.py:_accepted_status  no longer emits "applied to the game"; returns
          "accepted — returned to the engine to apply", or for a passed deadline
          "NOT applied — the engine's {N}ms deadline passed ... the game has applied its own
          fallback and moved on"
        AgentBrain waits on min(self.timeout, engine deadline) - ABANDON_MARGIN_SECONDS,
          floored at half the deadline, so it abandons FIRST and the existing
          Unanswered -> BrainError -> degrade path records honestly
        WorldView.decision_deadline_ms typed (not a passthrough extra — na-wzw's lesson),
          with 0/negative collapsing to None so "absent stays unbounded"
        DecisionQueue.await_answer returns that reason as the 409 body, telling the agent not
          to resubmit

  [4] "Correct the SKILL's 'no clock on your reasoning' line"
      DONE — SKILL.md:12 now reads "but only for llm_timeout_ms, and the built-in default is ...".

TESTS: full orchestrator suite 477 passed, 4 skipped, 0 failed. Targeted
`-k "abandon or deadline or pending or agent_brain or submit"` -> 37 passed.

RESIDUAL, documented rather than hidden — and it is why _accepted_status keeps its deadline
branch. The abandon margin (250ms) does not cover work that happens AFTER the answer is handed
over: grounding, the guard, and a possible repair. So a decision can still finish late. The
difference from the state this bead was filed in is that it is now REPORTED as late instead of
recorded as an applied llm decision. That is the defect this bead was about — silent and
flattering — and it is gone.

NOT CLOSED BY THIS, and deliberately not claimed: a pending from a genuinely DEAD game process
is a different failure — no deadline logic saves you when the run itself vanished. That is
na-bzd, which contract.py:264 calls "the companion to decision_deadline_ms and the half it
cannot cover", and it is partially landed already (b675d9d names the run so the orchestrator can
see the game die). Still open, still mine.

VERIFY BY MECHANISM, per this bead's own closing line: proof an agent decision landed is a
tier=llm row in the ADAPTER's na-observations.jsonl, or applied_item matching the agent's
choice — never the orchestrator's own record.

title: Play a turn with Claude Code driving via MCP
description:
Supersedes the transport half of na-ckn. Everything is built and verified without a game; this is the run that needs one.

  1. $SMAC_DIR present, 'just game verify' clean.
  2. thinker.ini: llm_factions=2, llm_endpoint=http://127.0.0.1:8000, llm_timeout_ms=0 (wait indefinitely).
  3. 'just play' — orchestrator with NA_BRAIN=agent.
  4. claude mcp add neural-amplifier, then let the play-alpha-centauri skill drive.
  5. Confirm: the game blocks at a base.production decision, next_decision returns a world view built from LIVE engine state, submit_orders changes what the base builds.
  6. Then kill the agent mid-decision with NA_AGENT_TIMEOUT set and confirm the game degrades to the deterministic tier instead of hanging.

Watch specifically for the window going 'not responding': the DLL slices its wait and calls PeekMessage(PM_NOREMOVE) without dispatching, deliberately, to avoid re-entering the engine from inside mod_base_build. If the window is unusable rather than merely stale, that trade needs revisiting - do NOT fix it by dispatching messages.
notes:
THE LOOP CLOSES. First adapter-side proof, 2026-08-02, live game:

  {'surface_id':'faction.se','turn':41,'faction':'Gaians','tier':'llm','applied':'llm','fallback_reason':None}

An attached Claude Code agent claimed a decision from a live engine via POST /agent/next, answered it via /agent/submit, and the ENGINE applied it. Verified in na-observations.jsonl (the adapter's own log), not in the orchestrator's - see na-t3h for why the orchestrator's record cannot be trusted for this.

Setup that made it work, all from step 2 of this bead: llm_factions=2 (Gaians, faction_id 1), llm_endpoint=http://127.0.0.1:8000, llm_timeout_ms=0. The last of those is load-bearing and the bead was right to name it: the built-in default is 2500ms and NO attached agent can meet it (na-t3h).

STILL OUTSTANDING for this bead:
  - Step 5 names base.production specifically. The surface proven is faction.se. The path is shared (na_decide_* -> na_http_post -> apply) so the mechanism is surface-agnostic, but the literal check has not been made: no tier=llm base.production row exists yet. Driving turns 41->42 produced no Gaians base.production decision, and the turn stopped advancing at 42 (the scripted TURN COMPLETE / confirm clicks stop working there - a unit awaiting orders, most likely).
  - Step 6 (kill the agent mid-decision with NA_AGENT_TIMEOUT set, confirm the game degrades rather than hangs) has NOT been run.
  - Step 4 used the HTTP agent endpoints directly rather than 'claude mcp add'. mcp_server.py wraps the same /agent/next + /agent/submit, so this is a thin difference, but it IS a difference and the bead says MCP.

Two operational traps found while doing it, both of which cost real time:
  - The orchestrator survives game restarts and keeps pendings from DEAD game processes, which then look like live work. Restart the orchestrator whenever you restart the game, and confirm /agent/waiting is empty before trusting the queue.
  - 'orchestrator unreachable or slow' is one message for two different causes (connection refused vs deadline passed). A decision that fired while the port was momentarily free is indistinguishable from one that timed out.

BASE.PRODUCTION REACHED THE LLM TIER (turn 42, Morgan Solutions, Morganites):

  adapter row: tier=llm, applied=llm_degraded, applied_item_name=Colony Pod

So step 5's transport half is proven on base.production, not just faction.se: the game blocked, /agent/next returned a world view built from live engine state (base_state, metrics, an eight-item action space with costs and both turn estimates, run_id, history), and the answer went back through the apply path.

BUT the choice did NOT change what the base builds, and the reason is a new P0: na-co2. StateGuard denied the entire action space because it reads minerals_remaining (a SHORTFALL - minerals still needed, 6 here) as a spendable budget, while every action declares effects of the full item cost (33). Every option therefore looks unaffordable by construction, the decision degraded, and the deterministic tier's pick was applied. `applied=llm_degraded` is the adapter recording that honestly.

So the state of this bead is now precise:
  - faction.se: FULLY closed loop, applied=llm, four times (turns 41, 42, and 1 of the stray run).

title: -na-autoload: exit the main menu after loading (menu-to-session transition)
description:
-na-autoload (thinker fork 2b82af5) successfully loads a savegame - mod_load_daemon returns SAVE_LOAD_VALID (status 0) against a real Autosave_<year>.sav, verified on the gaming host. But the game stays on the main menu, so the loaded state is unreachable.

Clearing *GameHalted is not sufficient. The engine does more of the menu-to-session transition inside load_game (engine.cpp:1057, address 0x5AAAB0) than state loading alone - probably tearing down the menu's own modal loop and entering the main interface. load_game takes (int, int) and addresses saves by slot, which is why it cannot be called directly for an arbitrary path.

Candidate approaches, cheapest first:
1. Identify what load_game does around its call to load_daemon (the call site is hooked at patch.cpp:639, address 0x5AAD7D) and replicate the surrounding steps. Disassembly of 0x5AAAB0..0x5AAD7D would answer it directly.
2. Find the menu's modal loop exit condition and set it alongside GameHalted.
3. Drive the menu with synthetic input instead. xdotool is installed and CAN see the Wine window ('Wine Desktop'), so sending the load-game keystrokes is feasible. Brittle and resolution-dependent, but it needs no engine RE and would unblock unattended runs today.

Approach 3 is the pragmatic unblock; 1 is the correct fix.
acceptance_criteria: Launching with -na-autoload <save> results in a playable in-game session with no human input; na-observations.jsonl shows base.production lines appearing without anyone touching the keyboard
notes:
Starting the QUICK START trace: the label 'QUICK START' does not appear as a string in terranx.exe, in any *.txt in the game directory, or in the 00000409.256 localization resource. So the startup menu is NOT a popp/Script.txt dialog - which rules out the cleanest intervention (intercepting the menu's popp call and answering it programmatically) and means the buttons are drawn from a graphical resource with the dispatch table in code.

Consequence: finding the QUICK START handler needs the menu's click-dispatch code located by structure rather than by string reference. Suggested route: the startup menu is drawn as a Console/Win, and gui.cpp already declares thiscall wrappers for the main-menu class at 0x5FB100 and neighbours (CMAINMENU_ADDSUBMENU_F etc.) - that class is the place to start, since whatever owns the buttons owns their handlers.

Note this does NOT invalidate the strategy in the previous note. Starting a game normally and then swapping state via the replay path is still the right shape; only the means of triggering 'start a game normally' is still open. If QUICK START proves awkward to invoke, any path that establishes a session will do, including a scripted new-game start.
close_reason: SOLVED. -na-autoload reaches a playable session unattended: click QUICK START (opens nothing modal), press Enter to confirm PLANETFALL, then run the engine's own replay/undo load sequence. Verified end to end with no human input - turn 35 from the target save, GameHalted clear, map rendered, no dialog. Key insight: stop constructing the menu-to-session transition and let the engine perform it, then swap state.

title: Verify Steam terranx.exe is Alien Crossfire v2.0
description: Run sha1sum against the Steam Planetary Pack install; want 4b19c1fe3266b5ebc4305cd182ed6e864e3a1c4a (3,084,288 bytes). Thinker refuses any other build. If it differs, the physical ISO plus the official v2.0 patch becomes the primary fixture source. Blocks every game-dependent lane. See docs/headless-harness.md section 2.
notes:
RESOLVED on gaming host (2026-07-29), but NOT by matching the hash.

Steam Planetary Pack (app 2204130), installdir 'Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri':
  terranx.exe  sha1 7bbcc54e64760c11a24f48862f15dbaaeab61435  3,094,576 bytes
  terran.exe   sha1 ca90a0776a5685a01c346e85fd23f3116ece975e  3,201,128 bytes
  PE: i386, 8 sections, link timestamp 1999-12-20 20:30:55 (original Firaxis build, not repacked)

This does NOT match Thinker's documented GOG anchor (4b19c1fe3266b5ebc4305cd182ed6e864e3a1c4a / 3,084,288) - it is 10,288 bytes larger.

It works anyway. Thinker Mod v5.4 is already installed in this directory and has driven a real
game against this exact binary:
  - debug.txt records 'ModVersion Thinker Mod v5.4 (Apr 29 2026)' / 'BinarySize 3094576'
  - saves/auto/ holds a continuous autosave run to Autosave_2234.sav (2026-06-20 19:25-19:56)
Since patch.cpp:218,250 verify original bytes before patching and abort on mismatch, reaching
turn-by-turn play proves every patch site in this build matches v2.0.

Conclusion: the na-8p9 premise ('Thinker refuses any other build') was an overstatement of the
source. Technical.md's own allowance - 'using other official game binaries of the same version
should also work' - is the operative rule, and the Steam build is such a binary. The hash is a
GOG-specific anchor, not a compatibility gate.

Consequence for the fixture (na-dyt): the manifest must record THIS host's hashes as the Steam
provenance line and must not hard-fail on the GOG anchor. Treat the anchor as one known-good
value among several.

Bonus, for na-ie9: it ran under Proton, not bare Wine. Prefix at
~/.local/share/Steam/steamapps/compatdata/2204130/pfx (ModuleName in debug.txt is the Wine
drive mapping S:\common\...). A working prefix already exists to build the Xvfb harness on.

# na-cjv slice 1 SHIPPED — why-view enrichment (9c7406e)

Took the "especially" first. Verified LIVE on the running dashboard, not just merged:
the deployed `/dashboard/api/decisions/609` now returns the `why` block.

## Two questions the panel could not answer, both failing silently

**1. Which directive bound the choice?** The panel rendered `in_force`, `followed` and
`overrode` as three flat lists. A directive in force and missing from `followed` reads as
"the model ignored it" — but MEASURED across 610 ladder-attempt4 decisions, `unsatisfied`
is populated on **609** and was rendered on **none**. So a reader saw four directives in
force, two followed, and no account of the other two.

Flat lists also hide that one directive appears in two lists at once: `followed+unsatisfied`
occurs **568 times**, and it is not a contradiction — `followed` means the model adhered
this turn, `unsatisfied` means the goal is not yet reached. One row per directive carrying
every disposition shows that; three lists structurally cannot.

**2. What grounding did it use?** Facts were not shown at all. Adding them needed care,
because THREE conditions produce an empty list and the orchestrator already tells them
apart:

| state | meaning | measured |
|---|---|---|
| `quipu_absent` | no retriever was configured — nothing was ever asked | ladder 610/610 |
| `quipu_degraded` | configured, and it FAILED | arm A 193/193 |
| empty | queried, matched nothing | — |

A single blank would have reported arm A's failed retrieval as a quiet healthy nothing.
Each state now gets its own badge and its own sentence, and retrieved facts are marked
with whether the brain actually cited them.

## Notes
- Computation is server-side and unit-tested, not expressed in the embedded JS string —
  that string has caused two prior defects in this file (na-uq1 x2).
- Both new guards proven by MUTATION: collapsing the grounding states, and dropping
  `unsatisfied` from the dispositions, each turn exactly the relevant tests red.
- 950 passed, 12 skipped. Diff scrubbed for internal identifiers with a positive control
  first (public repo).
- I checked one hypothesis and it was WRONG: I expected the panel was showing a thin
  top-level `reason` while the rich prose sat in `chosen[].reason`. Measured: they are
  identical in 610/610. The model's reasoning was already being shown correctly.

## Next slices
2. STRATEGY PANEL — directives in force per turn (starts_turn/active, checkpoints, adherence).
3. GRAPH VIEW — browse the NA quipu graph (3,742 triples on the NA store).

comments.text:
# na-cjv slices 2-5 shipped

## Slice 2 — STRATEGY PANEL (03edbca, LIVE, verified on :8088)
Per-directive adherence across the whole run, built from the decision log rather than a live
DirectiveStore: the log is the committed artifact and carries the disposition recorded at
decision time, whereas a store read answers "what is in force NOW" — a different question from
"what was in force at turn 42".

Live numbers from the ladder row: **73 turns, 8 directives**.

    expand-10-by-50           in force 345  followed 259  goal-unmet 345  share 0.751
    early-expansion-push      in force 345  followed 148  goal-unmet 115  share 0.429
    expand-20-by-80           in force 264  followed 110  goal-unmet 264  share 0.417
    arbitration-court-surplus in force 123  followed  25  goal-unmet  90  share 0.203

`followed_share` is over turns-in-force, **not** over followed+unsatisfied — those co-occur 568
times, so that denominator can exceed the population and would report a directive followed every
single turn as roughly half-followed. A test pins it.

Directive TEXT is reported as coverage, not just a source: a plan file being present does not
mean every directive has text — most are issued at runtime via `/agent/directive`. Live it reads
**0 of 8**, honestly, rather than eight blank cells.

## Slice 3 — GRAPH VIEW (a7a8dea, LIVE)
Census by type, semantic search, per-entity fact drill-down, read-only. Live against the NA
store: **345 entities across 10 types** (Technology 88, Facility 69, SecretProject 64…);
searching "colony pod" returns colony-pod top-ranked at 0.679.

A test asserts the panel can only reach `/query` and `/search` — a browse surface that could
reach `/episode` or `/knot` would let a viewer mutate the graph the brain decides from.

## Slice 4 — PLAIN LANGUAGE + PAUSED BANNER (f51d6c8, deploying)
From Stiwi's reading. Glossary defined once in Python so it is testable and the HTML cannot
drift: `degraded` → "Fallback — engine default used"; `tier=llm` → "LLM decided"; columns become
"Decided by" / "Action taken" / "Engine would pick"; dispositions carry their meaning on hover,
and `unsatisfied` says the genuinely confusing part — it is about the GOAL, not this choice.
A test asserts the word "degraded" never appears in anything the reader is shown.

The banner now has three distinct states. The old text was "IDLE SINCE <timestamp>", a fact about
the ARTIFACTS; on a row stopped 79 minutes ago it reads as a page that failed to load. It now
says: **"PAUSED // NO NEW DECISION FOR 79 MINUTES — the game reached turn 78 and stopped there.
The page is up to date; this is the game not running, not a broken page."**

## Slice 5 — the installer was going to erase all of this (6163b08)
Wiring the graph panel needed `NA_DASHBOARD_QUIPU` in `dashboard.env`. That file is REWRITTEN
from scratch by `install-dashboard-service.sh`, which emits exactly three keys — so the next
install would have silently dropped it, and the panel would have gone back to reporting
"unconfigured", an honest-looking state that hides a lost setting.

It had already bitten: `NA_DASHBOARD_GAME_STATE` is live in the deployed file and is not written
by the installer, so a re-install would have removed the all-player faction census with nothing
to say why. Fixed by preserving every unmanaged `NA_*` key — a mechanism, not a longer list, so
the next setting added is safe without the installer learning about it. Proven both directions.

## Open / not done
- **Directive text is unavailable in production.** `NA_DASHBOARD_PLAN` is unset and the ladder
  row's `plan.json` lives in an agent's ephemeral scratchpad, which is not a thing to point a
  service at. The panel says so rather than hiding it. If the directive prose should be visible,
  the plan file needs a durable home first — flagging rather than pointing production at /tmp.
- Visual graph rendering remains the stretch goal; this is the searchable list + per-node facts.
- Observed once: `tests/test_orders.py::test_batch_over_http` failed in 1 of 6 full-suite runs,
  passes in isolation and on the baseline. Order-dependent flake, not from these changes.

decisions and climbing, verified from its OWN decision log rather than the shared observations
file, because "the service is active" is not the claim "the run is advancing".

## Three attempts. Both failures were mine, and both came AFTER the gate was spent
1. **`--scope` instead of a detached unit.** Caught before launching, on malcolm's warning: a
   scope runs attached to the caller, so a pane death would have killed the run exactly as the
   timeout wrapper did in the morning.
2. **`THINKER_DIR`** defaults to `$REPO_ROOT/../thinker`. Arm B runs from the main checkout so
   that resolves; this arm runs from a worktree, one level deeper, so it did not. Died in 1s.
3. **No `NA_WINEPREFIX` / `SMAC_PLAY_DIR`.** The harness fell back to the default wine prefix
   and found the SHARED Steam install — so it started a game **in the directory arm B was
   playing in**, and the observations it read back were arm B's, at turn 103 with 47 bases while
   this arm is at turn 44 with two. It died in 7s on an unanswerable dialog ("Video player not
   found from MoviePlayerPath"). The dialog is what stopped it; sharing a board with a live
   experiment is what mattered.

a full gate pass including a real row-sized decision to learn something knowable in advance.

- **Double-lock deadlock** with malcolm's row probe: I locked in the gate, he locked in the
  probe. Both correct; composed, my gate held the lock and his probe waited 900s for it. A lock
  belongs at the resource, once — the probe owns the port and the unit, so it owns the lock.
- **A lock held on an inherited fd outlives the process that took it.** Killing the gate did not
  release it: the `tail` in its pipeline had inherited fd 9 and reparented to init.
  `ls -l /proc/*/fd` found the holder when the process list could not.
- **The watcher orphaned its gate** when stopped by PID. It traps now, proven green-with and
  red-without.

Arm A's orchestrator (pid 487926, port 8025) is in a **tmux-spawn scope** — pane-attached, from
its original launch. It survived tonight, but it is the same death class: if that pane dies, the
orchestrator arm A depends on dies with it. Flagging rather than restarting it under a live run.

comments.text:
# Two corrections to my 06:06Z report — one is an error I made

## 1. I killed the paused game while defusing the deadline. My mistake.

I SIGKILLed pid 488175 (the `timeout` wrapper) intending to remove only the wall-clock
deadline. 488175 was the process-GROUP LEADER. Killing it orphaned the group, and POSIX
requires the kernel to send SIGHUP+SIGCONT to an orphaned process group that contains
stopped members. So terranx.exe, wineserver and xvfb-run all took the HUP and died.
The freeze did not survive the defuse.

I should have either (a) killed the timeout from OUTSIDE by making the group non-orphaned
first, or (b) simply not used SIGSTOP as the freeze primitive when a wall-clock wrapper
was going to have to be removed later. The two mechanisms are hostile to each other and I
did not check that before acting.

### What this cost: nothing on disk. Verified, not assumed.
- boundary save byte-identical to the live ring copy (cmp, after cleanup)
- decision log still 193 records, unchanged from the pause
- autosave ring still 134 files, Autosave_2149 (turn 49) newest
- orchestrator :8025 healthy, game_id game-4b16d34d
- PRESERVED-529-storm-20260824/ intact and read-only

### What it cost in practice
The resume path changes from `kill -CONT` (continue in place at turn 49) to an autoload
restart from a save. Since the plan was already to restart from the turn-44 boundary with
a corrected retry budget, the practical loss is small. I am not offering that as an
excuse — if the plan had been "continue in place", this would have ended the run.

The 0945Z deadline IS defused: no timeout wrapper targets arm A any more (the surviving
`timeout 21600s` process belongs to ladder-attempt4 and was not touched). Resume is now
gated on upstream health as you asked, with no clock pressure.

Debris cleaned: zombie reaped, orphan Xvfb terminated, no arm A processes remain.
Control run ladder-attempt4 verified untouched and still advancing throughout.

## 2. Scope error: there is no ff7 arm B. My "arm A vs arm main" was not an A/B.

`ls na-runs/*ff7*` returns exactly one directory: na-ff7-arm-a. The row I called
"arm main" is **ladder-attempt4**, a different experiment, and it runs a DIFFERENT BRAIN:

    na-ff7-arm-a     NA_BRAIN=claude-code
    ladder-attempt4  NA_BRAIN unset (default brain)

So "the arms have different retry budgets" is not supported — I compared two unrelated
runs and described it as a confound between two arms of one experiment. Withdraw that.

### What survives the correction, and it is still the actionable part
Internally valid for arm A on its own numbers: 2 attempts per decision, 7.5% 529 rate,
7 of 80 decisions lost, turns 45-49 at 100/100/100/75/67% degraded safe-fallback.
A 2-attempt budget does not survive a 7.5% upstream error rate. That stands on arm A's
own data and does not depend on any comparison.

The 5-6 attempts I measured on ladder-attempt4 is evidence that a larger budget rides out
the same storm, but it is a different harness and brain, so treat it as suggestive, not
as a controlled result.

Recommendation is unchanged in direction, weaker in justification: raise arm A's attempts
before resuming, and resume from the turn-44 boundary. Whether 5-6 is the right number is
now an open question rather than something I have shown.

# Resume gate for arm A — upstream health, not clock

Sattler's ruling: resume is triggered by upstream HEALTH, not clock pressure.
The wall-clock deadline is gone (no timeout wrapper targets arm A any more).

## The gate

    scripts/upstream-529-health.py --minutes 15
      exit 0 = GO         529 rate <= 1.0% on a sample of >= 40
      exit 1 = HOLD       rate above threshold
      exit 2 = NO VERDICT sample < 40 — refuses to call it

It samples EVERY live Claude Code session transcript on this host, so it measures the
real upstream using traffic that is already happening. No probe request is issued and
no experiment's decision log is polluted — better statistics than one cheap decision
(hundreds of requests per window instead of one) and zero side effects.

**Why exit 2 exists.** A clean window and a DEAD window produce the same error count: zero.
Below the sample floor the gate refuses a verdict rather than reporting health. That is the
whole reason to trust a GO from it.

    GO         exit 0  threshold raised above the live rate (--go-rate)
    NO VERDICT exit 2  1-min window, sample 35 < 40

and would have shown a false 0. That defect bit me once in this session and is caught.)

comments.text:
# Standing order implemented — composed gate + autonomous resume

## Composition (sattler's amendment)
`composed-resume-gate.sh`
- PRIMARY: my statistical gate (passive transcript sampling, large N, zero cost).
- CONFIRMATION: malcolm's `upstream-probe.sh`, 5 consecutive OK — his script, invoked, not
  reimplemented. Composed, not raced: **the active probe only runs after the statistics clear**,
  so we never spend probes while the primary already says hold. Verified: current HOLD spent zero.
- exits 0 RESUME-READY / 1 HOLD / 2 NO VERDICT / 3 confirmation failed / 4 probe unavailable.
  Exit 4 matters — malcolm's probe lives in an ephemeral session scratchpad. If it vanishes the
  gate refuses to call it ready on one gate rather than silently degrading to primary-only.

## Resume (`resume-arm-a.sh`) — the four things the order specified
1. **Gate** must exit 0 (FORCE=1 documented, not default).
2. **Autoload by NAME** — `NA_SAVE=<turn-44 boundary>`. The harness copies a named save to
   `saves/fixture/loaded.sav`. Deliberately not NA_RESUME, which takes "newest by mtime" and
   would make the run depend on whatever else wrote to the directory.
3. **systemd-run --user --scope**, and `NA_TIMEOUT=` to disable the harness's own `timeout`
   wrapper. This is the direct fix for what killed the frozen run: a scope has a real lifecycle
   (`systemctl --user stop`) and never requires killing a process-group leader.
4. **Brain identity before the first decision** — and in two steps, because they are two claims:
   - `/health` reports the CONFIGURED brain (must be `claude-code`);
   - then exercise the brain's OWN path (`claude -p`) and read back the model that actually
     answered. A configured brain and a working one are different facts; only the second
     one is evidence. Aborts rather than starting a run on a dead brain.

## Watch (`arm-a-resume-watch.sh`) — running, pid logged to resume-watch.log
Polls the composed gate every 5 min and fires the resume itself. **Bounded: 4h deadline.**
If the deadline fires, that is a finding, not a timeout to retry — the storm outlasted the
window and arm A stays down pending escalation.

comments.author: ellie
comments.text:
# Defect in the composed gate: the confirmation step vetoes a HEALTHY upstream

Found while the gate held arm A down for 11+ minutes with the storm already over.

## The evidence
- PRIMARY (passive statistics): **0.00% 529s on a sample of 243-419**. Upstream is clean.
- CONFIRMATION (active probe): has not reached 5 consecutive OK in **678 seconds**.
- An isolated probe returned `OK 17218ms` at one moment and **exceeded 120s** minutes later.
- Dominant concurrent consumer: ladder-attempt4's brain
  (`NeuralAmplifier/orchestrator/.venv/bin/python3`), observed mid-call at **age 101s**; that
  workload makes calls in the 100-300s class.

## Why the confirmation cannot pass, by construction
`upstream-probe.sh` wraps its call in `timeout 120`. On expiry rc=124 with **both streams empty**,
so the reason string matches none of `529|overloaded|api error: 50[023]|...` and it classifies as
**HARD**. My `composed-resume-gate.sh` resets the consecutive counter on anything that is not `OK`.

So while a neighbouring experiment is making 100-300s brain calls, the probe's 120s ceiling is
**below the ambient call latency of the machine it shares**, and the confirmation can never reach
five in a row — regardless of upstream health.

## The actual design error, which is mine
**The confirmation step tests a different proposition from the primary.**

- primary asks: *is the upstream returning 529s?*  -> the thing we are gating on
- probe asks:   *did one call complete within 120 seconds?* -> a LATENCY question

I composed them as if they measured the same thing. They do not, so the strictly-tighter-looking
AND is not conservative — it is a veto on an unrelated signal. Under contention the probe's answer
is dominated by neighbours' load, which is exactly the variable the passive gate was chosen to be
immune to.

## Recommended fix (not applied — the composition was sattler's ruling)
Make the confirmation test the SAME proposition:

1. **Count only 529/overloaded as a confirmation failure.** A timeout or HARD result is *not*
   evidence of upstream 529s; log it, do not reset on it. This is a one-line change to the case
   arm and keeps the probe's real purpose.
2. Failing that, raise the probe ceiling above ambient max latency (300s+), or
3. Make confirmation ADVISORY: log its class, let the primary decide.

Option 1 is preferred: it is the smallest change and it fixes the category error rather than
tuning around it.

## Note on self-inflicted load
Three probe sources were live at once (malcolm's watch every 180s, this gate every 60s, plus my
manual checks). I stopped adding manual probes once I noticed. Probe-based watches are an active
load source and several agents running them independently is itself a contention source — another
argument for passive sampling as the primary.

comments.author: ellie
comments.text:
# Resume gate for arm A — upstream health, not clock (FINAL FORM)

No wall-clock deadline exists any more. Resume is triggered by health.

## The ladder — cheap to heavy, each tier paid for only once the cheaper signal is clean

    scripts/composed-resume-gate.sh

    TIER 1  PRIMARY   upstream-529-health.py — passive statistics over every live session
                      transcript. Hundreds of observations per window, zero cost, no
                      pollution, and no feedback loop (it adds no load of its own).
    TIER 2  LIGHT     malcolm's upstream-probe.sh — 5 consecutive OK under his 30s ceiling.
                      SLOW/TIMEOUT HOLD the streak; only a true 529 (REFUSED) resets it.
    TIER 3  ROW-SIZED malcolm's row-sized-probe.sh — ONE real ~13,474-byte decision.
                      Decisive. Serialised under /tmp/na-rowprobe.lock.

    exit 0 RESUME-READY | 1 HOLD (primary) | 2 NO VERDICT (thin sample)
         3 confirmation held (slow) | 4 probe unavailable | 5 HARD | 6 row probe rejected

## Why three tiers and not one

- **Exit 2 exists** because a clean window and a DEAD window both report zero errors. Below the
  sample floor the gate refuses a verdict rather than reporting health.
- **Slow holds, only 529 resets**, because the primary asks "is the upstream 529ing" while a fixed
  timeout asks "did one call finish in time" — a latency question dominated by other tenants. The
  first version ANDed those two propositions and held the run down 11+ minutes on a 0.00% upstream.
- **Tier 3 exists** because the light probe sends 30 bytes and a real decision sends ~13,474 — 449x
  heavier, and Overloaded is plausibly size-correlated. MEASURED: light probe `OK 9.2s` while a
  row-sized call took **6m39s and returned degraded on a 529**, same window. A missing row probe
  makes the gate REFUSE rather than fall back to the light gate.

## Resume procedure (automated — `arm-a-resume-watch.sh`, 4h deadline)
1. Gate exits 0.
2. `resume-arm-a.sh` re-checks the gate, then verifies the brain as TWO facts: `/health` reports the
   configured brain, then the brain's own `claude -p` path is exercised and the answering model read
   back. Aborts rather than starting a run on a dead brain.
3. Autoload **by name** — `NA_SAVE=PRESERVED-529-storm-20260824/BOUNDARY-turn44-clean-0449UTC.sav`
   (turn 44). Never NA_RESUME/newest-by-mtime, which would depend on whatever else wrote to the dir.
4. `systemd-run --user --scope` with `NA_TIMEOUT=` — no bare timeout wrapper. A scope has a real
   lifecycle; the previous run died because a SIGSTOP freeze met a wall-clock wrapper whose kill
   orphaned the process group.
5. Retry policy **attempts=2**, symmetric across both arms by sattler's ruling. Recorded in
   `CENSUS-EXCLUSIONS.json`.

## Exclusions
`CENSUS-EXCLUSIONS.json` — 2145-47 EXCLUDED-UNBRAINED (safe as engine baseline),
2148-49 EXCLUDED-MIXED (contains 3 genuinely brained decisions; NOT an engine baseline).

U.N. Liberty Haven held a **fully paid** Colony Pod (minerals_remaining 0, turns_to_completion 0)
at pop 1 for **15 base-turns**, and completed it on the exact turn its population reached 2
(turn 30->31, pop 2->1, build resets to 27). Same base, same paid pod, one variable changed. That
is as close to a natural experiment as this run offers.

So the cost of the constraint is NOT lost bases — it is **stalled production**. The gate is
already enforced below us; what we lack is the foresight to avoid parking capital behind it.
Gating on projected population, as Stiwi says, converts 15 dead base-turns into 15 turns of
Formers or growth.

AND IT SPLITS MY EARLIER ANSWER IN TWO — I owe a correction
I reported mineral surplus as THE binding constraint. That is right LATE and wrong as a summary.

    arm B  pod PAID and HELD at pop 1        15 base-turns   turns 13-44   POPULATION
    arm B  pod chosen at mineral_surplus 0   15 base-turns   turns 41-65   FUNDING

Raising the mineral floor would not have released Liberty Haven's pod: it was already paid for.
na-b8g needs both gates, not one.

of minerals and never blocked on population. It completed **three colony pods** — turns 24, 35

# na-b8g ITERATION 1 IS REFUTED BY ARM B'S OWN DATA — and the real constraint is not production choice

## My earlier prep on this bead is now STALE. Correcting it first.
I wrote that Formers ran 7.8% before turn 36 and 30.3% after, and proposed raising the Former
floor. **The directives to do that are already in force** (`hq-formers-before-pods`,
`rush-hq-formers-with-reserves`) and they WORKED:

    turns 0-99   Formers 51.2%   Colony Pod 41.1%     (779 choices resolved, 0 unresolved)
    turns 100+   Formers 38.3%   Colony Pod 61.7%

Formers went from 7.8% to **51% of early production**. The lever was pulled hard.

## And the economy did not move
    turn  75   bases 6   mineral_surplus 2   pop 13
    turn 105   bases 6   mineral_surplus 0   pop 18
    turn 151   bases 6   mineral_surplus 0   pop 19

Bases flat at 6 for ~76 turns. Surplus pinned at 0 for the last 38. So iteration 1's premise —
raise the production floor by building Formers — **has been tested and it failed.** It postponed
the flatline (from ~turn 36 to ~75) rather than removing it. Proposing more of the same would be
proposing a treatment that has already been administered.

## The finding: at zero surplus, EVERY production choice is a choice to build nothing
    turn 100+   turns_to_completion: None    minerals_remaining: 20    mineral_surplus: 0

`turns_to_completion` is **None** on every sample from turn 100 on. The item cannot finish. The
HQ has been holding "Formers, 20 minerals remaining" for fifty turns. Colony Pod is chosen 62% of
turns 100+ and `base_count` never moves, because a 30-mineral pod at 0 surplus never completes.

**This makes the production surface moot.** Decision quality cannot matter when the denominator
is zero — the agent is choosing correctly among items none of which can ever be built. Every
adherence and slope metric computed over turns 100+ is measuring a surface with no causal power.

## Where the minerals go (confidence: INFERRED, and the check is named)
    HQ base_state:  mineral_intake 4    mineral_surplus 0    pop_size 4    specialists 0

The base produces 4 and nets 0, so 4 are consumed before the build. In SMAC the standard sink is
UNIT SUPPORT, and `military_units` sits at 7-8 across 6 bases. Two directives already in force
target exactly this — `cap-military-support-drain` and `free-support-by-disbanding` — so a prior
pass reached the same suspicion. They are evidently not sufficient: military is still 7 and
surplus is still 0.

**This is INFERRED, not extracted.** intake−surplus=4 proves the minerals are consumed; it does
not by itself prove support is the consumer. The world view exposes no support field — `economy`
and `units` are both absent from the base.production view — so the adapter cannot currently
answer this, which is itself the gap to close first.

**And it makes iteration 1 self-defeating, which explains the failure:** a Former is a UNIT, so
building Formers to raise minerals ADDS support drain and lowers minerals first. At 6 bases the
lever fights itself.

Franklin's `smac-content-population-threshold` (at Transcend the 2nd citizen is a drone) is real
game knowledge but is **not** binding here: `drone_total` is 0.0 for the whole run and 1.0 at
turn 151 — the counter is proven live, so the zeros are real. The economy is not drone-eaten.

1. **PREREQUISITE, not optional: surface the support/upkeep number in the world view.** Right now
   the binding constraint is invisible to the brain and to us. No directive about support can be
   measured, followed or scored while the metric it names is absent — that is the
   exists-but-cannot-fire class. Do this before any arm.
2. Then target SUPPORT, not production: reduce units-per-base or raise free support, and measure
   `mineral_surplus > 0` as the primary outcome rather than base_count.
3. **Falsifiable prediction, written before the arm:** if support drain is the constraint, then
   cutting military units to <= 1 per base raises HQ `mineral_surplus` above 0 within 10 turns

   consumer is something else and this diagnosis is wrong.
4. Do NOT add another production-side directive until surplus > 0. Iteration 1 already showed

comments.text:
# na-b8g PREREQUISITE, specified — surface the support drain. No arm, no build, ready to land.

Done while rows are frozen (9fvnb). This is a spec, not an edit: thinker is a shared checkout
with a third-party upstream and a build change means a new row, which the ruling forbids.

## First, a precision correction to my own finding above
I wrote that `turns_to_completion: None` means "the game reports the item will never complete".
It is more deliberate than that. `src/neural.cpp:771-775`:

    // Omitted rather than guessed when the base cannot finish anything: a
    // zero here would read as "completes this turn", which is the opposite
    // of the truth (metrics.py: absent must never read as satisfied).
    if (b.mineral_surplus > 0) {
        na_buf_printf(w, ",\"turns_to_completion\":%d", ...);
    }

The field is **withheld on purpose** at surplus <= 0, precisely so an absent value cannot be
misread as satisfied. So the absence IS the signal, and it was designed that way. My conclusion
stands — at surplus 0 nothing completes — but the mechanism is an emitter that refuses to guess,
not an engine reporting infinity. Worth stating exactly, because "the field is missing" and "the
engine says never" would send a reader to different code.

## What is missing, and it is the binding constraint
`na_write_base_state` (src/neural.cpp:789+) emits pop_size, minerals_accumulated,
mineral_surplus, nutrient_intake, mineral_intake, energy_intake, eco_damage, worked_tiles,
specialists, queue_size. **Nothing about support.**

So the brain sees `mineral_intake 4, mineral_surplus 0` and cannot see where the 4 went. Neither
could I — I had to infer it. A directive about support (two are already in force:
`cap-military-support-drain`, `free-support-by-disbanding`) names a quantity that appears in no
world view, so it can be neither followed deliberately nor scored. That is the
exists-but-cannot-fire class, applied to a directive rather than an alert.

## The engine already computes it — three call sites, no new arithmetic
    src/base.h:51   int  mod_base_upkeep(int base_id);
    src/base.h:60   int  unit_support_free(int SE_support, int pop_size);
    src/base.h:59   int  unit_support_cost(int SE_support);
    src/engine_base.h:117   BaseSupportCosts[8][2]
    src/engine_data.h:138   SE_support

## Proposed emission — two fields, in na_write_base_state, next to mineral_intake
    ,"support_cost":<minerals consumed by unit support at this base>
    ,"support_free":<units this base supports at no mineral cost>

Deliberately two numbers and not a ratio, matching the emitter's own stated convention a few
lines up: *"Ships accumulated minerals and surplus separately rather than a pre-computed 'turns
remaining' … a number that is quietly wrong is worse than two numbers the brain can divide."*

**Follow the same absent-not-guessed discipline:** if upkeep cannot be determined for a base,
omit the field rather than emitting 0 — a zero here would read as "support is free", which is
the opposite of the truth in exactly the situation that matters.

## Why this must land before iteration 2 and not alongside it
The iteration-2 prediction is "cut military to <= 1 per base and HQ mineral_surplus clears 0
within 10 turns". Without `support_cost` that prediction can only be scored on its *outcome*
(surplus moved or not), never on its *mechanism* (support fell, therefore surplus rose). If
surplus does not move we would not be able to tell a wrong diagnosis from a directive that was
never followed — and iteration 1 already cost a full row to a lever that turned out to be
self-defeating. One emitted number separates those two outcomes.

## Verification when it lands (before any arm)
1. A base with known units shows `support_cost` equal to `mineral_intake - mineral_surplus`
   when support is the only sink — and where they differ, that difference is itself the finding.
2. Positive control: a base with zero units supported must emit `support_cost: 0`, not omit it.
   Omission is reserved for "cannot determine".

comments.text:
# SPEC AMENDED — two fields are not enough. The SUPPORT RATING must ship with the cost.

sattler's connection to franklin's `smac-mineral-support-cost-constraint` (6czy9, from alphax.txt
#SOCSUPPORT) changes the spec, and it does so by making my own inference TESTABLE rather than by
confirming it. Read from the graph directly:

    -4  costs 2 minerals per unit, no free support for a new base
     0  gives 2 FREE units per base
    +3  gives 4 units, or up to base size, free
    Police State and Power raise SUPPORT; Democratic lowers it, Thought Control heavily.

## This nearly refutes my diagnosis, and that is the point
Arm B has **6 bases and 7-8 military units**. At SUPPORT 0 that is **12 free** — comfortably
more than 8. So on the default rating, support should cost nothing and my "support is eating the
4 minerals" inference would be WRONG.

Three ways it can still be right, and they are distinguishable only with the rating in hand:
1. the faction's SUPPORT rating is NEGATIVE (Peacekeepers + a Democratic-leaning social choice),
2. non-military units count — **Formers are supported units too**, and iteration 1 pushed Formers
   to 51% of early production, so the true supported count is 8 military PLUS the former fleet,
3. the diagnosis is wrong and something else consumes the 4.

Note that (2) would make iteration 1 self-defeating in a second, sharper way than I wrote
earlier: it did not merely add units, it added units *past a free allowance* — which is where
the cost turns on.

## Corroboration found, and its limit stated
The world view's `directives[].intent` text, written by a previous agent, already says
*"All six bases report 0 mineral surplus while 8 military units draw support"* and *"nets 0
minerals after support"* (twice). So an independent observer reached the same read.

**That is corroboration, not measurement.** They almost certainly computed it the way I did —
`mineral_intake - mineral_surplus` — so this is two people running the same inference, not two
instruments agreeing. It raises confidence in the arithmetic and adds nothing about the cause.
The rating is what separates them.

## Amended emission — THREE fields, not two
    ,"support_cost":<minerals this base pays for unit support>
    ,"support_free":<units supported at no mineral cost, i.e. the allowance>
    ,"se_support":<the SOCIAL SUPPORT rating, -4..+3>       <-- ADDED

`support_cost` alone is a snapshot of a quantity whose driver is invisible: the same number means
different things at different ratings, and the remedies diverge completely. If the rating is 0
and units exceed the allowance, the fix is **disband or stop building units**. If the rating is
negative because of a social choice, the fix is **change SE**, and disbanding treats a symptom
while the structural cost stays. The two live directives (`free-support-by-disbanding`,
`cap-military-support-drain`) both assume the first without being able to check.

Same absent-not-guessed rule as `turns_to_completion`: omit any field that cannot be determined
rather than emitting 0, since 0 reads as "support is free" — the opposite of the truth in the one
case that matters.

## Wiring, per sattler
Once the fields exist, the iteration-2 directive cites
`smac-mineral-support-cost-constraint` rather than restating the mechanic, so the game knowledge
lives in the graph and the directive references it. **Ship in the SAME thinker build as the
9fvnb council fix — one new-row boundary, not two.**

## What this does to the iteration-2 prediction
The prediction gains a discriminating clause it did not have:
- if `se_support >= 0` and supported units exceed the allowance -> cutting units clears surplus;
- if `se_support < 0` -> cutting units will NOT clear it and the lever is social engineering.
Either way the measurement now distinguishes them, which is what iteration 1 could not do.

comments.author: malcolm
comments.text:
## FIXED and DEPLOYED — two defects, both frontend, neither on the suspect list (confidence:extracted)

`main` is at **4c2baa9**; the deployment checkout is pulled to it and `neural-amplifier-dashboard.service` restarted. Rendered proof: `~/workspace/na-runs/proofs/na-uq1-dashboard-fixed-20260824T0028.png`.

**The screenshot shows** the banner reading `LIVE // TURN 66 // 470 DECISIONS`, MISSION CONTROL populated (`game-29a893f2`, turn 66, 470 decisions, difficulty talent, slot human), FACTION STATUS showing Peacekeepers, 100 rows in DECISION ARCHIVE, and the EVALUATION DATALINKS tables rendered — that last one matters most, because `renderEvals` is the function that was broken.

### Defect 1 — Python ate the JavaScript newline escapes

`DASHBOARD_HTML` is a plain triple-quoted string, so a `\n` written for JavaScript is consumed by **Python** and emitted as a real newline. A JS regex literal cannot span lines, so `renderEvals`'s `split(/\n(?==== )/)` reached the browser unterminated. Three occurrences, all on one line. `\\S` and `\\d` on that same line are correct, so the double-escape was understood and three `\n` were missed.

**A SyntaxError anywhere in an inline script means the WHOLE script never executes.** `refresh()` was never defined and never ran, so every card, panel and row stayed empty on a page whose backend was serving live rows the entire time.

Browser console at 04:19, before the fix:

```
[    1216ms] Invalid regular expression: missing /
```

Control pair, same extraction, `node --check`: **PASS** on the fixed script, and on the served one:

```
SyntaxError: Invalid regular expression: missing /
```

### Defect 2 — `status` is not the element

Found while proving defect 1 in the browser, and it is why defect 1 was invisible.

`window.status` is a legacy **string** property, so the bare identifier `status` resolves to it and `status.textContent = ...` assigns to a throwaway String wrapper and is silently discarded. Measured in the page: `(0,eval)('status')` returns `""` with `typeof "string"`, and `bare === document.getElementById('status')` is **false**. Every other id here — `summary`, `factions`, `decisions`, `evals`, `detail`, `detailText` — resolves to its element; only this one collides with a built-in.

So the banner could never leave `LINKING…`, and — the expensive part — `catch(e){status.textContent='LINK DEGRADED // '+e}` could never display anything either. **The page had no channel to report its own failure**, which is exactly why a hard JS error reached a human as "the dashboard shows no data".

Caught in the act: after defect 1 was fixed, the banner still read `LINKING…` while `summary` held `TURN 65` and the decision table held **100 rows**. Fixed by binding `statusEl` once, rather than renaming the id, which the CSS keys on.

### On the filed suspects — all three REFUTED

| suspect | measured |
|---|---|
| (1) fetch paths broken relative to `/dashboard` | no: paths are absolute `/dashboard/api/...`, and both endpoints answer in ~35ms |
| (2) JS chokes on a post-restore field shape | no: the script never ran at all, so no field was ever read. It renders the 3-game_id log fine |
| (3) stale cached page | no: a cache-busted URL reproduced it identically. **Stiwi should still hard-refresh now** — his tab holds the genuinely broken page |

### Why nothing caught this

`test_dashboard.py` asserted `"function renderEvals" in response.text`. That is true of a script that cannot parse. **Presence is not validity.** Six substring assertions passed against a page that rendered nothing.

Two tests added, both sabotage-checked against the unfixed source (fail), with the six older tests still passing (which measures how blind they were):

- `test_the_page_script_actually_parses` — extracts the inline script from the served page and runs `node --check` on it, plus three node-free assertions that the escapes survive as two characters rather than a line break.
- `test_the_status_banner_is_addressed_by_a_binding_and_not_by_a_bare_id`.

Full suite: **912 passed, 12 skipped** on the merge candidate.

title: Attempt 4 cannot reach its 250-turn cap inside its own 21600s timeout — measured kill 04:36, projected arrival 04:54+
description:
Attempt 4 (`ladder-attempt4`, arm na-ff7-long-form-b, seed 1) is configured with `-na-exit-turn 250` inside a `timeout --kill-after=30s 21600s` wrapper. **The turn cap cannot be reached inside the timeout.** Structural, not a channel fault; the na-xl3 outage merely made me measure it.

MEASURED 2026-08-24 00:05 (confidence:extracted):

- The wrapper is PID `2918787`, `PGID 2918787` = terranx's PGID (`ps -o pid,etimes,lstart,pgid`). Started `Sun Aug 23 22:36:00`. `21600 - 5146 = 16454s remaining` -> **SIGTERM at 04:36:00**.
- Observed rate at turn 55: `55 turns / 82.7 min = 0.665 turns/min`. Holding that rate CONSTANT, turn 250 arrives at **04:54** — 18 minutes AFTER the kill.
- That constant-rate figure is optimistic twice over: it includes the 5 free unbrained auto-advanced turns (49-53), and the cost per turn is rising monotonically.
- Decisions per turn, from `orch/decisions.jsonl`:

  | turns | mean decisions/turn |
  |---|---|
  | 0-9   | 3.40 |
  | 10-19 | 6.10 |
  | 20-29 | 7.40 |
  | 30-39 | 8.90 |
  | 40-48 | 9.78 |

  Each decision is one LLM call (median latency 5.7s, p90 12.1s — na-xl3). The plan in force mandates 20 bases by turn 80 and 40 by turn 110, and `base.production` is per-base, so decisions/turn keeps climbing. The rate will FALL, not hold.

- Turn 140 — the last entry in `manifest.json.census_turns` `[50,55,80,91,110,140]` — arrives at **02:10** at constant rate, and still lands inside 04:36 even if the per-turn cost DOUBLES (04:18). **The census schedule completes; the 250-turn cap does not.**

So the row will be SIGTERMed somewhere past turn 140 and short of 250, and a reader of the results file will see a truncated run rather than a declared limit.

Options (recommendation: B):
- A. Raise `timeout` for future attempts to cover the measured cost curve rather than a flat 6h guess.
- B. **Declare the row's real deliverable as the census schedule through turn 140** and record 250 as unreachable at this cost curve, so the truncation is a stated bound instead of a failure. Cheapest, needs no relaunch, and the census turns are what the arm was built to measure.
- C. Relaunch with a longer timeout — throws away 55 turns of paid work and re-incurs them.

Cannot be fixed on the running row: `timeout`'s deadline is fixed at exec. Any change applies to the next attempt.
close_reason: Premise discharged + durable fix landed 8351359: NO_PROGRESS_LIMIT=3h replaces the wall clock. The '8.16 min/turn slowdown' was an artifact - PRE/POST medians are 2.43/2.38, three outage turns held 73% of the window. Cap set ABOVE the 107.5min measured RECOVERABLE stall (43 BUSY, 0 STALLED) because a tighter no-turn-advance cap kills a row that recovered. 6 arms, 4 sabotages fail, 989 pass.

comments.author: malcolm
comments.text:
## EXTENDED per sattler's ruling — the live row is no longer wall-clock bounded (confidence:extracted)

`timeout --kill-after=30s 21600s`, PID `2918787`, `PGID 2918787` = terranx's PGID. `timeout`'s deadline is fixed at exec and cannot be lengthened, so the wrapper was **defused** rather than extended: `kill -9 2918787` at `00:04:36`. SIGKILL cannot be caught, so `timeout` died without forwarding anything to its child and without running its group-kill.

Verified immediately after, in the same command:

```
timeout 2918787: GONE
2918815    3965 Xvfb            <- alive
2919173    3965 terranx.exe     <- alive
heartbeat: 2026-08-24 00:04:35   (1s old)
```

and three minutes later the row was at turn 58 with both units active. `xvfb-run`'s `/bin/sh` (2918789) exited with the timeout; `Xvfb :101` survived and did NOT get torn down by its cleanup trap, which is the outcome this needed.

**A correlation I nearly published as a cause, and it was wrong.** 40 seconds after the kill the driver logged a **5-consecutive** no-result streak — the run's worst, against a previous maximum of 2, one short of `SILENT_LIMIT`. The obvious story is that the kill perturbed the channel. It did not. The window `00:05:16-00:07:14` is covered end to end by four turn-57 `base.production` decisions of **29.5s / 26.7s / 47.7s / 15.8s = 119.7s**, the 47.7s being the run's longest, with worldview writes at 00:05:35, 00:06:02, 00:06:56 and 00:07:12 proving the brain was working throughout. It is na-xl3's own cause, measured harder. Recorded here because the wrong version was one edit away from being the record.

Also recorded on the row manifest under `wall_clock_cap`, with the authority and the rationale.

## The durable fix: cap on PROGRESS, not on wall clock

The 6h number was a guess about how long a row takes, and the quantity it was guarding is "is this run still getting anywhere" — which wall clock cannot see. It fails in both directions:

- **False kill** (what happened here): a healthy row is 18 minutes short and gets SIGTERMed.
- **False patience**: a row wedged at turn 3 keeps a game, an Xvfb and a paid brain alive for the remaining 5h58m, which is the zombie case the cap exists for and the case it is worst at.

Proposed shape, to sit where `timeout` sits today:

- Kill on **no turn advance for N minutes**, not on total elapsed. The driver already tracks `stuck` (cycles since the turn last moved) and already knows the turn, so the signal is in hand.
- N must be scaled to the measured per-turn cost, not fixed: decisions/turn rose **3.40 -> 9.78 across turns 0-48** and the plan mandates 20 bases by turn 80, so a turn late in a row legitimately takes several times what an early one takes. A fixed N that is safe at turn 5 is a false kill at turn 200.
- Keep a wall-clock backstop, but set it far above any plausible row rather than at the row's expected length — a backstop that fires in the normal case is not a backstop.
- The same evidence the na-xl3 classification now gathers (game heartbeat advancing vs frozen) distinguishes "slow" from "wedged" and belongs in this decision too.

Not implemented on this row: changing the cap mechanism mid-row is exactly the class of perturbation that cost turns 49-53. It is the next attempt's launcher change.

comments.author: malcolm
comments.text:
## The wall-clock cap was the wrong constraint to worry about — CONTENTION is (confidence:extracted)

Measured 01:30, turn 77. The timeout is defused, so the row now has unlimited wall clock and still cannot reach 250.

| window | n | degraded | median | p90 | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| turns 0-48 (pre-outage) | 346 | 0 (0%) | 5.8s | 12.9s | 42.9s |
| turns 55-70 | 174 | 5 (3%) | 7.0s | 21.0s | 47.7s |
| **turns 74+** | 38 | **9 (24%)** | 9.6s | **199.6s** | **281.6s** |

**The median barely moved and the tail exploded.** 9.6s median against a 63.6s MEAN. Projecting from the median gives 5.0 hours to turn 250; projecting from the mean gives **33 hours**. The mean is the honest figure here because the tail is where the time actually goes, and the row is charged for it. At 10.8 decisions/turn and 173 turns remaining, the row is not slow, it is infeasible.

**Cause, and it is not the row's:** `claude -p` is exiting 1 with an EMPTY stderr on 24% of recent decisions. `claude_account_status` reads **critical — 11 active sessions, 5.6h token remaining**, five_hour 17%, seven_day 46%. My row's brain issues one `claude -p` per decision and is competing with the whole crew for one account; two concurrent `claude -p` processes were observed.

**What this changes about na-cp5.** The bead argued the cap should be progress-based rather than wall-clock, and that stands — but for a new reason. A no-turn-advance window would have caught THIS too, and a wall-clock cap would not: the row is advancing, just at 1/7th the rate it was costed at, and no elapsed-time bound distinguishes "slow because contended" from "wedged". Both need the same signal.

**A capacity fact worth carrying past this row:** a ladder row's cost model was built on a ~6s decision. That figure is only valid at low fleet concurrency. It is not a property of the row — it is a property of how many agents are running, which the row cannot see and does not record. A published row should carry the concurrent-session count at launch, or its latency numbers are not comparable to another row's.

Related defect found while measuring this, filed as **na-bql** (P1): `/coverage` records a degraded fallback as `tier=llm, model=claude-code` and reports `llm_decisions 599/599, deterministic 0` while 19 of them had no model output. So the instrument that certifies the row's provenance cannot show the contention at all.

Not stopping the row. The decision to continue, re-cost or abandon is sattler's, and the game state is intact either way.

comments.author: malcolm
comments.text:
## The retry I landed is COUNTERPRODUCTIVE at this failure rate, and I deployed it into a storm

Recorded against myself, because the effect is the opposite of the one the change was made for and nothing in its tests could have shown it.

`c3ff10b` retries a transient upstream failure once. That is correct at a LOW failure rate: one 529 in twenty decisions becomes a real decision instead of a `safe fallback`, for a few seconds. At a HIGH failure rate it inverts — each retry doubles the cost of a decision that then fails anyway, and the game thread is blocked throughout. The failure rate when I deployed it was 50-67% on the last handful of decisions. So the change was right in the direction it was reasoned about and wrong in the regime it was shipped into.

**The regime, measured from turn first-seen times in `turns.log`:**

```
71  00:39:31
72  00:41:25     }  2.1 min/turn across 71-76
73  00:43:37     }
74  00:45:36     }
75  00:48:02     }
76  00:50:09     <-- 529s begin here
77  01:21:29     31 minutes
78  01:49:48     28 minutes
    (78 still open 8 minutes later, 2 decisions in that window)
```

**A 14x slowdown, and it starts exactly at the turn the 529s start.** At ~30 min/turn the 172 remaining turns are **86 hours**. The row is not slow, and it is not merely infeasible against a wall clock I already removed — it is producing roughly two contaminated turns an hour.

## What the tests could not have caught, which is the transferable part

The fourteen arms prove the retry fires on a 529, does not fire on a quota wall, is bounded at one, and leaves its counter at zero on a clean call. Every one of those is a per-decision property, and all of them still hold. **The defect is a per-RUN property**: whether retrying raises or lowers throughput depends on the ambient failure rate, which no single-decision test has access to. A change whose correctness is conditional on a rate cannot be validated by a suite that only ever sees one call.

The honest fix shape, not implemented: make the retry conditional on the *observed recent* failure rate — retry while failures are rare, stop retrying once they are common, since at that point the upstream is telling you to back off rather than press. That is a circuit breaker, and it is the difference between "retry transient errors" and "retry transient errors while that is still cheap".

## Recommendation, superseding both of my earlier ones

- ~~stop at 75 because of local contention~~ — retracted, wrong cause (529 is upstream; the account had 17%/46% headroom).
- ~~wait, it is transient~~ — true of any single 529 and not of this hour: eight minutes produced zero turns.
- **PAUSE at the frozen turn-75 boundary.** `Autosave_2175.sav` is already copied read-only into `clean-boundary-turn75/`, so the clean segment cannot be lost. Pausing means stopping the driver AND the game — stopping only the driver is not a pause, because `-na-auto-turn 60` then plays the row unbrained, which is precisely how turns 49-53 were lost tonight.

Not doing it unilaterally: it ends a live game process. The state is intact either way, and `Autosave_2177` (turn 77) also exists if a contaminated resume is ever wanted.
