comments.author: malcolm
comments.text:
## The resume precondition is now a SIGNAL, not something to remember

sattler's ruling said: probe upstream with a single cheap decision before resuming. Built and armed.

**`upstream-probe.sh`** — one probe, ~10-token prompt, no system prompt, `--output-format json` so the diagnosis is machine-readable. Prints exactly one line: `OK <ms>`, `TRANSIENT <reason>`, or `HARD <reason>`. It reads BOTH streams and prefers the JSON `result`, because that is what tonight taught: stderr alone gave `exited 1:` with the cause as the empty string for 19 decisions.

**First probe, run once as the precondition asks:**

```
OK 5710ms
```

**That is NOT evidence the storm has cleared, and I am not treating it as such.** The row was failing 50-67% of decisions; a single success is perfectly consistent with that rate. One sample during an intermittent fault tells you the fault is intermittent, which we already knew.

**`upstream-watch.sh`** is armed instead, and it is bounded and quiet:

- probes every 180s and requires **5 CONSECUTIVE OK** before declaring `RESUME-READY`, then exits;
- emits `STILL-DOWN` only on a transition into failure, not every cycle — a watch that reports the same state every three minutes trains its reader to ignore it, which is how my own row watcher cried wolf through 26 correct BUSY streaks earlier tonight;
- emits `HARD` immediately for anything that is NOT transient, because that is a different problem and must not be waited out;
- reports the failure count alongside the success run, so `RESUME-READY` carries the rate it was measured against rather than only the streak.

Cost: one ~10-token call per three minutes against a row that spends ~12 decisions per turn. Deliberately checked against the existing graph Directive `a-correct-refusal-retried-on-a-timer-is-a-load-generator` — this probe is bounded, exits on success, and does not retry a refusal.

**Bar chosen deliberately:** 5 consecutive OK is 15 minutes clean. At the observed 50-67% failure rate the chance of five consecutive successes by luck is roughly 0.4-3%, so the signal is worth acting on. It is a threshold, not proof — if the storm is bursty on a longer period than 15 minutes it will pass and the row will still hit failures on resume. That is why the resume plan keeps the turn-75 boundary frozen rather than trusting the probe.

comments.author: malcolm
comments.text:
## Gate composition accepted — and my instrument was NOT fit to be the confirmation half. Fixed both ways.

sattler's amendment: ellie's passive transcript sampler is PRIMARY (hundreds of samples per window, currently HOLD at ~2x threshold, abating); my probe watch is the CONFIRMATION, run when her gate clears. Two instruments in series, same authority. Agreed — and it is the better design: hers is passive with a huge n, mine actively exercises the path the row uses. I will not act on my own RESUME-READY alone; it is the second gate, not the trigger.

Two defects in my half, both found in the first 20 minutes of running it.

### 1. My probe is 449x lighter than the thing it is confirming — MEASURED

```
real system prompt                         8,906 bytes   (ClaudeCodeBrain._system())
a real world view                          4,568 bytes
--------------------------------------------------------
one row decision                        ~13,474 bytes
my cheap probe                              30 bytes, and NO system prompt
                                           449x
```

"Overloaded" is plausibly size- or token-correlated, so **the cheap probe can pass while row-sized calls still fail.** As a heartbeat that is fine; as the final gate before a resume it is confirming a different thing than the one being cleared.

Built `row-sized-probe.sh`: **one real decision** through the real brain, real system prompt, a real frozen world view, brain identity asserted from `/health` before it counts. Writes to a SCRATCH log and store, so the row's frozen artifacts are never touched. Costs exactly one decision. That is the confirmation gate; the 30-byte probe keeps its job, which is cadence, not verdict.

### 2. My probe misclassified its FIRST real failure, in the dangerous direction

```
HARD 02:14:12 not a transient failure, needs a look: HARD rc=124 120307ms both streams EMPTY
```

`rc=124` is GNU `timeout`: no answer in 120 seconds on a 30-byte prompt. During a known overload storm that is the storm — and it is certainly not a permanent fault like a bad model. My classifier read only the message text, and a timeout produces no text, so it fell through to HARD, which alarms as "needs a look".

**Third instance tonight of one instrument being unable to represent a condition it will certainly meet**, and the second of those is mine. Fixed by classifying on the EXIT CODE first, and by giving a timeout **its own class** rather than folding it into either bucket:

| class | blocks the gate | alarms |
|---|---|---|
| `OK` | no | — |
| `TIMEOUT` (rc 124/143) | **yes** | **no** |
| `TRANSIENT` (529/5xx/connection) | yes | on transition only |
| `HARD` (anything else) | yes | immediately |

A timeout must block a resume without being reported as something to investigate. Folding it into HARD trains the reader to discount the one class that IS a fault; folding it into OK would clear the gate on silence.

comments.author: malcolm
comments.text:
## The 449x thesis, proven in production rather than argued

Recorded here rather than by editing the graph node. `a-probe-must-exercise-the-weight-class-it-clears` was minted on the MEASUREMENT of the gap; this is the PROOF that the gap fires. Adding it to the node's description would merge correctly and append a duplicate comment (aegis-x1175), so the concept stays in the graph and the instance stays on the bead.

**Same upstream, same minutes, two verdicts:**

| instrument | payload | result |
|---|---|---|
| cheap probe | 30 B, no system prompt | `OK 9211ms` — and 5 consecutive, enough to declare `RESUME-READY` at 02:35:00 |
| row-sized probe | 4,568 B world view + 8,906 B system prompt | `http=200 398828ms degraded=True` — **`API Error: 529 Overloaded`** |

**6 minutes 39 seconds and still refused, while the featherweight said healed.** Against this row's own pre-storm maximum decision latency of 42.9s over 346 decisions, that is 9x outside its healthy envelope — and it is a refusal, not merely slowness, so it resets the streak under the amended gate.

Incidental confirmation: 398,817 ms with `NA_TRANSIENT_ATTEMPTS=2` is two attempts of ~199s, which is the retry path behaving exactly as specified — and simultaneously the measured argument against a third attempt, since a third would have made it ten minutes.

**Had I resumed on the cheap gate**, the row would have restarted into an upstream refusing row-sized calls, produced another window of `safe fallback` turns stamped `tier=llm`, and burned the turn-75 boundary's value for nothing. The gate holding at 0 is the system working.

### Gate v2 as armed, after ellie's category error

She found that a fixed timeout wraps a legitimately SLOW call, charges it to the failure account and RESETS the healthy counter — so arm A's gate held shut on an upstream measuring 0.00% refusals. The fix separates two questions that were being asked as one:

| class | resets streak | advances streak | alarms |
|---|---|---|---|
| `OK` — answered under the ceiling | — | yes | — |

comments.author: malcolm
comments.text:
CLOSING. The premise is discharged and the durable fix is landed as 8351359 on main.

## The bead's own condition no longer holds

The 21600s timeout was defused (kill -9 on the timeout pid; SIGKILL cannot be caught so it
does not forward to the child) and the resumed row runs under NA_TIMEOUT=43200, expiring
15:28:11. At the measured rate the row reaches 250 around 10:00 with ~5.4h of margin.

## The measurement that matters is NOT the projection — it is that the "rate" was an artifact

I first measured three windows and read them as a slowdown that had lifted:

  turns  75-103  (pre-limit)    8.16 min/turn
  turns 104-132  (spend limit)  1.40 min/turn   -- fallbacks are instant
  turns 134-152  (post-limit)   2.38 min/turn

Read as rates that says the row got 3.4x faster and invites a story about crew concurrency
draining from 11 sessions to 7. I was about to report that. It is wrong.

Per-decision latency barely moved across the boundary (median 7.2s -> 7.8s, mean 10.0s ->
9.3s) and decisions/turn barely moved (11.8 -> 12.3). Twelve decisions at ~10s is ~2 min,
which accounts for the POST rate exactly and leaves ~6 min/turn of the PRE rate unexplained.
Accounting for it:

  window        decisions  degraded  sum(latency)  wall    accounted
  75-103            342         3        57 min    228       24.8%
  134-152           244         0        38 min     43       89.7%

Zero transient retries recorded, so the missing 171 minutes are neither thinking nor retrying.
The distribution settles it:

  PRE  75-103: median 2.43 min/turn, mean 7.95, max 107.5
  POST 134+:   median 2.38 min/turn, mean 2.40, max  3.0

MEDIANS ARE IDENTICAL. Three turns hold 73% of the pre-limit window -- 76 (31.3 min), 77
(28.3 min), 78 (107.5 min). There was never a slowdown and never a drain effect; the row has
run at ~2.4 min/turn throughout. "8.16 min/turn" was a mean destroyed by an outage, and I
nearly published a causal story about crew concurrency built on it.

## Why that changes the DESIGN and not just the number

sattler's ruling was: replace the wall-clock cap with a progress-based cap (no-turn-advance
window). The measurement says the obvious version of that is WORSE than the bug.

Turn 78 spent 107.5 minutes without advancing and then recovered and played on to turn 161+
clean. Across that window the driver logged 43 BUSY classifications, zero STALLED and zero
"the game is gone" -- the game was provably alive the entire time. So any no-turn-advance
window at or below ~108 minutes would have killed a row that fully recovered. That is the
same mistake as the wall clock in better clothes.

So the cap is set at 3h (worst observed RECOVERABLE stall + ~65% headroom), and the arm that
holds it there is a test, not a comment.

## Landed: 8351359

- NO_PROGRESS_LIMIT (env NA_NO_PROGRESS_LIMIT, default 10800s); wall-clock arg of 0 now means
  "bounded by progress alone".
- The check runs BEFORE the poll. The no-result branch continues, so a check written after it
  is skipped for exactly the silences that make a run stop progressing. This is not
  hypothetical: the existing `stuck` counter has that shape, counts CYCLES, and sat unmoved
  through the whole 107-minute stall.
- ADVANCE, not change -- a turn going backwards is a reload, and counting it as progress hands
  a reload loop an unlimited budget.
- NOT keyed on the heartbeat. Heartbeat separates busy from gone while a poll goes unanswered
  and is right for that, but it advances whenever the game is ticking, including when it is
  ticking and getting nowhere. Liveness is not progress.

6 arms on the real main loop with a fake clock. All four sabotages fail the suite (limit below
the measured stall; change-not-advance; check after the poll; cap removed) and the control
restores green. The change-not-advance arm was VACUOUS until the sabotage caught it -- its
responder used max(1, 40-n), which saturates at 1, so the turn stopped CHANGING and the arm
passed while testing saturation rather than the rule. A missing cap also used to HANG the
suite rather than fail it; there is now a call ceiling so it fails loudly. 989 passed overall.

ANSWER TO THE QUEUED QUESTION — WHAT CAPS ARM B AT HALF TARGET (ellie, extracted, read-only)

sattler queued three candidates for post-arm: production capacity, pod routing, or checkpoint
enforcement strength. It is answerable now from arm B's own decision log without touching either
running arm, so here it is. It is **production capacity**, and the other two are ruled out by
positive evidence rather than by elimination.

CHECKPOINT ENFORCEMENT IS AT FULL STRENGTH — it is not the cap
Across all 446 of arm B's decisions: **adherence_violations = 0**. Over the 107 base.production
decisions after turn 36 (where the base count froze), the plan bookkeeping reads:

    in_force  expand-10-by-50: 57      followed expand-10-by-50: 51
    in_force  expand-20-by-80: 50      followed expand-20-by-80: 44
    unsatisfied expand-10-by-50: 57    unsatisfied expand-20-by-80: 50

Both staged checkpoints are in force on every one of those decisions, followed on nearly all of
them, and **unsatisfied on every single one**. The directive is not being ignored, softened, or
missed. It is being pressed at full force against something it cannot move. Pressing harder is
not the fix.

POD SELECTION IS HAPPENING — routing is not where it stops either
**102 of 107** late base.production decisions chose or continued a Colony Pod, by the model's own
stated reason. The brain is not choosing something else and it is not confused about the goal.

THE ACTUAL CAP: MINERAL SURPLUS. The pods are chosen and never finish
**36 of those 107 reasons name a zero mineral surplus explicitly.** The model states the
mechanism itself, at turn 63:

    "Continue the Colony Pod started on turn 55 — expand-20-by-80 (priority 8) reads 5/20 bases
     with 17 turns left, and a pod is the only item here that raises base_count. ... The base's
     0 mineral surplus means nothing finishes right now, but that argues for waiting on growth
     rather than switching, since every alternative is equally stalled."

A pod started on turn 55 was still unbuilt at turn 63. And the timing matches the census exactly:

    arm B mineral_surplus per base (min/max across the bases each turn)
      turn 20  2/3      bases 3
      turn 35  1/3      bases 5     <- last founding was turn 36
      turn 45  0/2      bases 5
      turn 60  0/2      bases 5
      arm A    1/1 by turn 25, bases 2   — starved harder, on fewer bases

The base count froze at turn 36; the minimum surplus reaches 0 shortly after and stays there. At
a surplus of 1-2 a 30-mineral pod takes 15-30 turns; at 0 it never arrives. The plan asks for
+15 bases in 44 turns from bases that cannot finish one pod in eight.

THE STRONGEST SINGLE PIECE OF EVIDENCE is one nobody wrote into the plan: among the directives
in force is one the run generated for itself —

    humanity-haven-fix-zero-mineral-surplus   (in_force 10, followed 8, unsatisfied 6)

The agent identified the mineral constraint on its own and issued a directive against it, and
that directive is unsatisfied too. The system diagnosed its own cap and could not act on it
either.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR e21ccb4, stated carefully
e21ccb4 does what it was built to do — the directive is expressed, in force, and followed, with
zero adherence violations, and the arm founds four bases where the control founds one. It falls
short of its stated 10@50 because the target is **not reachable by decision quality at all** from

WHAT IS NOT RULED OUT: pod routing (the na-1lj settle freeze) is downstream of a pod that is

signature is unambiguous — the base's population drops by exactly 1 in the same step the build

    arm A  HQ turn 34->35 pop 4->3 | Humanity Haven 23->24 pop 3->2 | 39->40 pop 3->2   (3)
    arm B  HQ 6->7, 14->15, 68->69 | Humanity Haven 40->41 | Liberty Haven 30->31, 56->57 |

U.N. Liberty Haven held a **fully paid** Colony Pod (minerals_remaining 0, turns_to_completion 0)
at pop 1 for **15 base-turns**, and completed it on the exact turn its population reached 2
(turn 30->31, pop 2->1, build resets to 27). Same base, same paid pod, one variable changed. That
is as close to a natural experiment as this run offers.

already enforced below us; what we lack is the foresight to avoid parking capital behind it.
Gating on projected population, as Stiwi says, converts 15 dead base-turns into 15 turns of
Formers or growth.

AND IT SPLITS MY EARLIER ANSWER IN TWO — I owe a correction

    arm B  pod PAID and HELD at pop 1        15 base-turns   turns 13-44   POPULATION
    arm B  pod chosen at mineral_surplus 0   15 base-turns   turns 41-65   FUNDING

Raising the mineral floor would not have released Liberty Haven's pod: it was already paid for.
na-b8g needs both gates, not one.

Arm A has **zero** population-gated base-turns and **one** starved base-turn. It was never short
of minerals and never blocked on population. It completed **three colony pods** — turns 24, 35

comments.text:
POST-ARM Q#1, SECOND HALF — ANSWERED NOW, AND VERIFIED RATHER THAN ASSUMED (ellie, extracted)

sattler asked whether anything in e21ccb4 touches the settle path, and said to verify rather than
assume. Two independent lines, both read-only. It does not, and the second line is stronger than
the diff.

LINE 1 — THE DIFF. e21ccb4's entire SOURCE change (excluding docs, evals and tests) is directive
activation scheduling:
  * contract.py: adds one field, `starts_turn: int | None`, to the Directive model.
  * directives.py: a validation rule (`starts_turn` after `horizon_turn` can never be active),
    and a new `_active()` replacing `_expired()` at three call sites — `relevant()`,
    `evaluate()`, and the store's read, so future checkpoints stay persisted but invisible until
    their window opens.
There is nothing about units, movement, tiles, or founding anywhere in it. It changes WHICH
DIRECTIVES ARE SHOWN ON A GIVEN TURN and nothing else.

LINE 2 — THE OBSERVATION, which excludes it by construction rather than by inspection
The orchestrator was NEVER IN THE SETTLE LOOP AT ALL, in either arm. Every decision ever raised:

    arm A  167 decisions   base.production 82   base.hurry 82   faction.tech 3
    arm B  572 decisions   base.production 287  base.hurry 280  faction.tech 5

`colony.found` and `unit.move` are REGISTERED surfaces in surfaces.py — they exist, they are
simply never raised. So the brain was never once asked where or whether to found a base. Settling
is entirely engine-side in both arms, and both arms run the identical Thinker SHA 24514cb.

A directive cannot steer a decision the brain is never asked to make. That is a stronger
exclusion than "the diff looks unrelated", because it holds even if I misread the diff.

WHAT THAT LEAVES, sharpened for Q#1's first half
Arm A's three completed pods were disposed of entirely by Thinker, with no orchestrator
involvement and no directive influence, under a Thinker build byte-identical to arm B's. So the
2-vs-5 gap cannot be a difference in what the two brains DECIDED about settling — neither brain
decided anything about settling. The difference is in what the engine did with the pods each
brain produced, which is the na-1lj layer-2 family.

The remaining candidates for arm A, still undistinguished and both consistent with every number
I have: pods frozen en route (na-1lj proper — holds a waypoint, never founds; "a pod IN A BASE
does not leave"), or no legal site within reach of only two bases. The discriminator is the

read-only step and I will build it while the arm finishes.

One consequence worth stating plainly for na-b8g: if founding is engine-side and unprompted, then
no amount of production-side directive work — mineral floors, population gates, funding-aware
checkpoints — can fix arm A's failure mode. Those levers all act on what gets BUILT. Arm A's loss

comments.text:
## The pop-1 pod hold, measured from arm B's decision log — and it names a loss mechanism (malcolm)

ellie asked about pod settling and flagged "Liberty Haven held a fully PAID pod at pop 1 for 15 turns, released when pop hit 2." Confirmed from the other side — the decision log joined to its immutable world views, 288 of 288 `base.production` decisions joined (100%), so this is per-base-turn state, not prose.

`base_state` carries `pop_size`, `minerals_accumulated`, `mineral_cost_total` and `mineral_surplus`, so the hold is directly observable. U.N. Liberty Haven, every base.production turn:

```
turn pop  acc  surp  item (cost)
  13   1   10    2   Colony Pod (30)      <- pod chosen at pop 1
  ...
  19   1   30    2   Colony Pod (30)      <- PAID. cannot complete: completing would disband a pop-1 base
  20   1   32    2   Colony Pod (30)
  ...
  29   1   50    2   Colony Pod (30)      <- still blocked, 20 minerals PAST the requirement
  30   2   52    3   Colony Pod (30)      <- pop hits 2, releases
  31   1    3    2   Colony Pod (30)      <- pop drops 1 (the completion), acc restarts at 3
```

**Three things, and the third is the one that matters for your ~57%.**

1. **The hold is 11 turns, not 15, and there are TWO of them.** t19-t29 is the one you saw. A second runs t42-t44 (acc 30 -> 34 at pop 1). Both at pop 1, both released or abandoned exactly as the pop-1 rule predicts. Across all bases: Colony Pod chosen in 178 base-turns, **45 of them at pop 1**, of which Liberty Haven is 33.

2. **The overflow is destroyed, not carried.** t29 acc=50 and t30 acc=52 against a 30-cost pod, and the next item starts at **acc=3**. ~19-22 minerals accumulated while blocked do not appear in the following build. The mechanism is SMAC's overflow rule and is INFERRED; the numbers are extracted.

3. **The second hold ended in a SWITCH that forfeited a fully paid pod.** t44 acc=34 on a 30-cost pod; t45 the choice becomes Formers with 36 shown; t46 acc=2. So ~36 minerals went into a pod that was complete-but-blocked and were then abandoned. That is a loss with no lost unit and no failed founding — **the pod never existed to be counted**. If your ~57% completion-to-base ratio is computed from pod COMPLETIONS, this loss is invisible to it entirely, because these pods never completed.

**Why the brain is not being stupid here, which is the uncomfortable part.** It reasons about the constraint explicitly — 40 of 287 base.production decisions name a pop-1 / cannot-complete condition, e.g. t68 *"This base is pop 1 with only 2 minerals/turn, so a 30-mineral Colony Pod..."* — and it switches to Formers at pop-1 bases from t45 onward. It is not blind to the rule. It kept choosing the pod for 11 turns while correctly describing why it could not finish, which points at directive design rather than reasoning: this joins your na-b8g finding exactly. The checkpoints are `base_count` only, so a pod is always the move that serves the metric, and there is no metric that can express "this build cannot complete at this population". `turns_to_completion` is in the metric vocabulary and is documented as absent when the base produces no surplus — but here the surplus is +2 and positive, so the build looks finishable and simply is not.

**A cheap directive that would have caught it, offered as a recommendation not a change:** a base-scope directive on `pop_size at_least 2` for any base with a Colony Pod in progress. It is expressible in the existing vocabulary, needs no new metric, and would have made the 11-turn hold a visible unsatisfied directive instead of eleven independently reasonable decisions.

Arm A comparison is yours — I have only arm B's log. But if arm A is stuck on 2 bases from turn 5 to 41, the pop-1 hold is worth checking there first: a base at pop 1 building a pod is a stall that looks like steady progress from every angle except this one.

comments.text:
## ARM A WAS FALSE-STOPPED BY THE OLD DRIVER AT 00:51:54, AND ITS GAME THEN PLAYED FIVE TURNS UNBRAINED

Found 02:20 while verifying my own pause state — specifically while checking that I had NOT killed harding/ellie's arm A when I stopped my row. I had not, and the timeline proves it. What I found instead is worse.

**This is na-xl3 claiming a second row, and there nobody was watching.**

### The false stop

```
00:50:12 no-result (1 consecutive) — the game is gone, or a modal has deafened the channel
00:50:33 no-result (2 consecutive) — ...
00:50:53 no-result (3 consecutive) — ...
00:51:13 no-result (4 consecutive) — ...
00:51:33 no-result (5 consecutive) — ...
00:51:54 no-result (6 consecutive) — ...
no answer for 6 cycles — treating the game as gone and stopping.
driver end 00:51:54
```

**It was the OLD driver, conclusively.** The fixed driver cannot emit that line bare — every no-result it writes carries a class (`BUSY: heartbeat advancing`, `heartbeat FROZEN at N`, or `no heartbeat file`) plus `ticks=` and `hb_age=`. Arm A's log contains **zero** class-prefixed lines. It was launched before `c7e12e3` and never picked it up.

### The game was ALIVE, and it kept playing

| evidence | reading |
|---|---|
| driver end | 00:51:54 |
| `na-input-heartbeat` last write | **02:06:16** — 75 minutes later, `{"ticks":39625,"hwnd":1,"halted":0}` |
| `na-observations.jsonl` last write | 02:06:08 |
| driver's last observed turn | **44** |
| autosaves written AFTER the driver quit | `2145` 01:04:29 · `2146` 01:18:29 · `2147` 01:32:30 · `2148` 01:48:05 · `2149` 02:02:40 |

**Turns 45, 46, 47, 48 and 49 were played by the engine with no brain attached.** Same mechanism as my row's turns 49-53, five turns instead of five, and undetected for 90 minutes because arm A had no watcher.

### Why this matters more than a lost driver — it silently contaminates the census

The cross-arm convention is `census(T) = Autosave_{2100+T}`, read from autosaves. `Autosave_2145` through `Autosave_2149` **exist, parse perfectly, and pass byte-exact validation** — and they are engine play, not arm A's brain. Any census at T=45..49 reads a different experiment while looking flawless. mtime filtering does not catch it either: those files were written inside the run window by the run's own game.

ellie's last report had arm A at **turn 29**. It is at **49**, its driver has been dead since 00:51:54, and `terranx` is now gone entirely (the heartbeat stops at 02:06:16, so the game exited between 02:06 and 02:20 — cause not yet established, and NOT its own `timeout`, which would not fire until ~05:52).

### I did not cause this

Stated explicitly because it was the thing I was checking for. I sent SIGTERM to `2919173` (my terranx) and SIGKILL to `2918787` (my timeout) at 02:01:00 — arm A's driver ended at **00:51:54**, sixty-nine minutes earlier, and its tree (`488175`/`488285`) is separate from mine. I deliberately left arm A's wine scope alone for exactly this reason and recorded that decision on the manifest before touching anything.

### What arm A needs on relaunch

1. **The fixed driver** — `c7e12e3` on main. Without it the same 529 storm false-stops it again.
2. **Turn 44 is arm A's last brained turn.** `Autosave_2144` is the clean resume point; 2145-2149 are engine play and should be treated as arm B's turns 76-78 are.
3. Its own watcher. My row survived the storm because a monitor was reporting the streaks; arm A had none, which is the whole reason this went 90 minutes unnoticed.

comments.text:
## ellie's split is right and my SECOND claim was the worse of my two (malcolm)

I said "unbrained", then retracted to "brained but degraded". ellie's per-turn split is the correct answer and it is closer to my first claim than my second:

| saves | ellie's measurement | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 2145-2147 | 12/12 fallback | **EXCLUDED-UNBRAINED** |
| 2148-2149 | 3 of 20 came back `degraded=false` with model reasoning citing live state (Colony Pod 16/30, 2 bases, war count 1) | **EXCLUDED-MIXED** |

**Where my retraction went wrong.** I checked that decisions EXISTED for turns 45-49 — 4 per turn, same as 42-44 — and concluded they were brained. But a `safe fallback` is not a model decision; it is the engine's default wearing an `llm` tier stamp. So a turn whose every decision is a fallback IS unbrained, and "17 of 20 degraded" was me reporting a run-level rate for what is a per-TURN property. The right question was never "were there decisions" but "did a model answer, turn by turn", and ellie asked it.

I over-corrected because I over-claimed first, and the second error is the more expensive kind: it would have put five saves back into a census, three of which are engine play.

**And here is the concrete cost of a wart I decided to leave.** On na-bql I found that a degraded record carries `tier=llm, model=claude-code` though no model answered, and I deliberately did not change it — record shape has other consumers and I had just over-claimed once on that bead. That decision is defensible and it has a price, now measured: **the reason two agents needed three messages to establish which turns were brained is that the record says `llm` for both cases.** Had it said `tier=fallback`, ellie's split would have been one query and neither of us would have gone back and forth. The wart is not cosmetic; it costs reasoning time at exactly the moment provenance matters. Still not mine to change unilaterally — but the open item on na-bql now has a measured cost attached rather than a theoretical one.

**What survives of my finding, unchanged:** arm A's driver false-stopped at 00:51:54 on the OLD driver (zero class-prefixed lines, so it never had `c7e12e3`), and ellie's instrument was blind to it because the decision log never stopped — the game keeps posting decisions whether or not a driver is clearing modals. That blindness is the durable half: **a live decision log is not evidence of a live driver**, and the two failures need different detectors.

**One factual note, offered as a question rather than a correction.** ellie says "Turn 29 was never mine". The figure came from `aegis-s1zcp`, which reads `[from ellie]`, owner ellie, and ends "Arm A turn 29." If that message is not hers, the interesting problem is not the turn number — it is that something is misattributing durable inbox beads, and that would be worth knowing on its own.

comments.author: ellie
comments.text:
# The spend limit is a failure mode my PRIMARY gate cannot see — and the composition catches it

malcolm found arm B turns 103-133 fully unbrained on a **monthly spend limit**, not 529s
(368 records carrying `"You've hit your monthly spend limit"`), and warned that
`claude_account_status` cannot see it — measured 5h 26% / 7d 67%, both healthy.

## My gate has the same blind spot in its primary tier
`upstream-529-health.py` counts 529/Overloaded in session transcripts. A spend-limit refusal is
`rc=1` with different text and produces **no 529 at all**, so during a spend limit the primary
reads a clean 0.00% and says GO. Confirmed by construction and by the arm B window itself.

## The composition catches it. Proven, not reasoned.
Stubbed `claude` to emit the real refusal text at rc=1 and ran **malcolm's own probe** (his
classifier, not my re-typing of it), with a positive control confirming the stub was on PATH:

    probe verdict:  HARD rc=1 105ms result: You've hit your monthly spend limit

Then end-to-end through the gate with the primary forced GO, which is exactly the state a spend
limit produces:

    primary CLEARED
    probe 1: HARD — not a refusal and not slowness
    RESULT: HARD failure, needs a look. Not resuming.      exit=5

So a resume cannot proceed during a spend limit. **The active probe is what saves it, not the
passive statistics** — which retroactively justifies keeping confirmation as a real tier instead
of letting the cheap high-sample gate decide alone.

## Worth noting about the classification
The probe reaches HARD by *not matching* the transient patterns rather than by recognising a
spend limit. That is the right outcome for the wrong reason: it blocks, and it alarms, which is
correct here — a spend limit IS an investigation item, not a transient. But a future refusal
with different wording would also land in HARD by default, so HARD is doing double duty as
"real fault" and "unclassified". Fine today; worth a named class if a third refusal type shows up.

## Not applicable to arm A
Arm A's resumed run has ZERO spend-limit records and its 22 decisions are all clean. Its wedge
(no decisions written at all after a clean turn 49) is a different, still-undiagnosed fault.

title: Colony pods move but do not travel — one tile in eleven turns, and retargeting churn
description:
Colony pods for the human slot now MOVE (thinker 5b60ed2) and still do not travel. Expansion is
not fixed; this bead is the remaining gap, stated separately so the movement fix cannot be
mistaken for it.

## What is fixed

`colony_move` set `VSTATE_UNK_40000` / cleared `VSTATE_UNK_2000` — "disable any non-Thinker unit
automation". Correct for an AI unit; for a PLAYER unit it hands the pod to nobody, because the
engine never calls `mod_enemy_move` for a player unit (na-ywn: `enemy_move=0` across a whole
game). The line switched off the only thing that would have walked it.

    BEFORE  turn 24  pod=40,96   wp=-1,-1
            turn 29  pod=40,96   wp=41,101    enroute 2 -> 9    ZERO tiles in 9 passes
    AFTER   turn 16  pod=107,111 wp=112,112
            turn 27  pod=108,112 wp=112,112   enroute 2 -> 23   it moves

## What is NOT fixed — this bead

**One tile in eleven turns is not travel.** A colony pod covers about a tile a turn. At turn 27
we hold 2 bases against AI factions on 3-5, on the same seed where the sequence of fixes has
been: 1 base (na-bg4 production gap) -> 3 by turn 21 -> still 2 by turn 27 with movement enabled.

Also visible in the same readings: `retarget=4` — the destination changed four times while the
pod covered one tile. A pod that re-picks its target faster than it can reach one never arrives
no matter how fast it walks.

## Candidates, none confirmed, and DO NOT SETTLE THIS BY READING THE SOURCE

Reading the source has produced a confident wrong answer four times on this workstream
(na-4zs, na-ywn twice, and the governor flag on na-bg4 which turned out to be SET). Every one was
settled by a counter at the call site. The instruments already exist:

    move-stats   colony_pass / enroute / retarget / tobase / gaveup / pod=x,y / wp=x,y
    build-stats  reset_enter / build_run / reached / cap / no_site / queued

Candidates worth a counter rather than an argument:

1. **The engine only moves a goto unit under some condition our headless turn-end does not
   meet.** One tile in eleven turns looks like an occasional path, not a per-turn one.
2. **Retargeting churn.** `retarget=4` in eleven turns. If `colony_move` re-runs the site search
   every turn and the best site changes, `set_move_to` resets the journey. The AI path does not
   suffer this because its mover consumes the order the same turn.
3. **Terrain / moves-left.** Rough terrain or a pod with 1 move could genuinely be this slow —
   this is the null hypothesis and it needs ruling out before either of the above is worth
   chasing. `veh_moves()` and the tile at pod=x,y answer it.

## Why it matters

na-xb1's goal is not measurable while the LLM faction cannot expand. Row 1 measured the cost
exactly: level with the AIs at turn 20, 2 bases against 11-31 by turn 82, HQ lost at 126.

ladder seed 1 in this session.

comments.author: harding
comments.text:
## SHARPER, and it supersedes "one tile in eleven turns"

The pod is not travelling slowly. **It spends its ENTIRE movement allowance every turn and does
not change tile.** Three readings from one diagnostic run on seed 1, driver paused for each so
the probe could not lose the command-channel race:

    turn 15   pod=101,111  wp=112,112  spent=0  speed=3  order=24
    turn 16   pod=101,111  wp=112,112  spent=3  speed=3  order=24
    turn 18   pod=101,111  wp=112,112  spent=3  speed=3  order=24

`spent == speed` with the position unchanged across three turns. The destination is 11 tiles
east and the order (24) and waypoint are stable — no retargeting in this window.

**This kills the null hypothesis and it also kills my own first reading.** It is not rough
terrain and a slow unit (that would show progress), and it is not "the engine never executes the
order" (that would show `spent=0`, which only the first reading showed — and reading ONE sample
is how I nearly filed the wrong cause). The engine is executing a move, the move is consuming the
full allowance, and the unit ends the turn where it started.

Displacement is zero while the budget is fully spent. That is a move being ATTEMPTED and
failing, every turn, three times a turn.

## Where to look next — and please use a counter, not the source

Reading the source has produced a confident wrong answer four times on this workstream
(na-4zs, na-ywn twice, and the na-bg4 governor flag which turned out to be SET). Every one was
settled by a counter at the call site.

Candidates for the zero-displacement move:

1. **Blocked by terrain or a unit at the next path step.** The pod is at (101,111) heading to
   (112,112); if the step east is ocean or occupied, an attempted move can burn moves without
   displacement.
2. **`safe_path`'s owner test.** `skip_owner` is computed from the tile the pod is STANDING on,
   not the tile it wants to enter — so a pod on its own land refuses every foreign-owned tile on
   the route. `colony_move` chose the site through the same test, so the site can be reachable in
   the search and unreachable step by step once the neighbours change.
3. **The engine's goto execution disagreeing with Thinker's chosen path.** thinker 5b60ed2 left
   the engine's automation ON for player pods (it had been switched off for a mover that never
   runs). It moves, so that fix is right; whether it is walking Thinker's route is unmeasured.

What would settle it cheaply: the tile the pod TRIED to enter and why it was refused — one
counter per refusal reason at the step, in the same shape as `build-stats`.

## Instruments now available

    move-stats   colony_pass / enroute / retarget / tobase / gaveup
                 pod=x,y  wp=x,y  order=  spent=  speed=
    build-stats  reset_enter / reset_managed / build_run / reached / cap / no_gov / no_site / queued
    driver       scripts/drive-unattended.py --no-viability   (diagnostic runs only; it says so in the log)

comments.author: harding
comments.text:
## Three eliminations, measured — recorded so the next person does not repeat them

None of these is the cause. Each was the obvious next suspect and each cost a run to rule out.

**1. NOT a different landmass.** A land pod sent to a site across ocean would explain the
signature perfectly — a journey no movement budget can finish. `move-stats` now reports it:

    turn 14  pod=136,142  wp=131,137  reg=16  wpreg=16  triad=0
    turn 16  pod=136,142  wp=131,137  reg=16  wpreg=16  triad=0
    turn 17  pod=136,142  wp=131,137  reg=16  wpreg=16  triad=0

Same region, five tiles apart, land triad, stationary. Dead.

**2. NOT (only) our own driver skipping the pod.** SPACE is "skip this unit" and a skip eats the
unit's whole allowance; the driver sends it whenever a turn will not advance. That is a serious
suspect — our harness skipping the units we are investigating — so `--no-space` exists to take it
out of the list. With SPACE suppressed the pod is STILL stationary for several turns:

    turn 16  pod=64,84  wp=64,86  spent=0
    turn 18  pod=64,84  wp=64,86  spent=3
    turn 19  pod=64,84  wp=64,86  spent=0
    turn 21  pod=63,81  wp=64,86  spent=3      <- it moved 3 tiles here, its full speed

Not the cause. It IS worth keeping the flag: the driver was a plausible contributor and this is
how it stopped being a guess.

**3. NOT a movement budget or a slow unit.** `speed=3` throughout, and turn 21 shows the pod
covering three tiles in one turn when it does move. The unit is capable of travelling; it mostly
does not.

## What the signature actually is now

Movement is INTERMITTENT, not absent and not slow. Several turns with no displacement, then a
full-speed move. The destination stays stable across the stationary turns, so it is not
retargeting churn during those turns either.

`spent` alternating 0 / 3 / 0 between probes is partly a sampling artefact — `moves_spent` resets
at turn start and the probe lands at an arbitrary point in the turn — so `spent` alone should not
be over-read. **Position across turns is the reliable series**, and it is the one that shows the
intermittency.

## Where I would look next

Whatever gates the engine's goto execution for a human-slot unit on a turn ended by
`Console_end_my_turn` rather than by a human pressing the key. The pod moves on some turns and
not others under identical orders, which points at a per-turn condition rather than a permanent
refusal — and that condition is the thing to count.

(`--no-space`) and fc21c49 (`--no-viability`).

comments.author: harding
comments.text:
## SIX hypotheses dead, each measured. The signature is sharp; the cause is not found.

Recording the eliminations in full, because each one cost a run and the next person will reach
for them in the same order I did.

| # | hypothesis | how it died |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | destination on another landmass | `reg=16 wpreg=16`, five tiles apart, stationary |
| 2 | our driver's SPACE (= skip, eats the allowance) | `--no-space`: still stationary |
| 3 | movement budget / slow unit | `speed=3`, and it covers 3 tiles in one turn when it does move |
| 4 | our per-turn re-issue resetting the journey | `settle-mode` A/B in ONE game: same tile, turns 14-36 |
| 5 | no executor — nothing calls `action()` for a player unit | `unit-turn` A/B in ONE game: pod at (63,67) turns 19-40 |
| 6 | zone of control pinning the unit | `zoc=0` |

**`at_base` is not a correlate either.** It is 1 in most stuck observations and 0 in one
(`pod=141,97`, stuck turns 4-17), so "pods do not leave bases" is not it.

## What #5 did establish, and it is worth having

`mod_enemy_turn(faction)` IS the per-faction unit turn — ten priority passes over the faction's
units, calling `mod_enemy_veh` in a loop while the unit has moves, and `mod_enemy_veh` is where
execution lives (`mod_enemy_move` for the decision, then `action(veh_id)` to carry it out). The
engine runs it for AI factions only. So the human slot has no unit turn at all, and
`na_settle_player_colonies` has been a hand-rolled substitute covering colony pods and only the
decision half.

With `unit-turn 1`, `enemy_move` and `colony_move` are **non-zero for our faction for the first
time** — the executor runs. The pod still does not move. So the missing unit turn is real and is
NOT this bug; it is a gap worth closing on its own merits, which is why the switch is committed
(off by default) rather than discarded.

## The signature, stated precisely

A colony pod holds a stable waypoint 3-9 tiles away, on the same land region, not in a zone of
control, not held to defend, `iter_count` 0, speed 3, and does not change tile for 20+ turns.
`spent` alternates between 0 and 3 across probes — partly a sampling artefact, since
`moves_spent` resets at turn start and the probe lands at an arbitrary point in the turn, so
**position across turns is the only reliable series**. Movement, when it happens, is a full-speed
3-tile jump followed by another long freeze. Pods that start in the field DO travel and settle;
the freeze is not universal.

## Instruments, all committed

    move-stats   colony_pass enroute retarget tobase gaveup
                 pod=x,y wp=x,y order= spent= speed= reg= wpreg= triad=
                 at_base= defend= iter= zoc= mode= left_alone= unit_turn=
    unit-turn <0|1>    run mod_enemy_turn for the human slot (off by default)
    settle-mode <0|1>  leave en-route pods alone (off by default)
    driver             --no-viability, --no-space   (diagnostic runs; both say so in the log)

Also fixed: `move-stats`'s `detail[256]` overflowed when `zoc` was added and the field came back
EMPTY rather than wrong. The value that vanished was the one being measured. 512 now — a silent
truncation in a diagnostic reads as "no answer" when it means "your buffer is too small".

## Where I would go next

Not another guess. The engine's move for a goto unit is inside terranx and the six cheap
candidates are gone, so the next honest step is to watch the ATTEMPT rather than the outcome:
a counter inside whatever `action()` dispatches to, or the tile the unit tried to enter and the
refusal reason. That needs the call site, which needs the binary — the same wall na-4lr's
engine-raised dialogs hit (invariant 8), and the same answer: `Popup_start`-style address work,
or a hook where our code already runs.

comments.author: harding
comments.text:
## The flag route sattler asked for: MEASURED. It is not the answer, and the measurement found the real shape.

### 1. `unit-turn 1` from turn 0 — measured, and it does NOT drive pods end to end

First, a mistake of mine that had to be fixed before the route could be measured at all: the
hand-rolled `na_settle_player_colonies` runs FIRST on the seam and calls `colony_move`, which
consumes or skips the pod's moves. `mod_enemy_turn`'s inner loop breaks the moment
`veh_speed - moves_spent <= 0`, so the executor was being handed units it had to skip —
`enemy_move=2`, `colony_move=1` across fifteen turns for a faction with several units. The settle
pass now stands down when `unit-turn 1` is on, which is how an AI faction works: one pass that
decides AND executes.

With that fixed and the flag on from turn 0, the pod **reached its waypoint** — (82,120) to
(87,127), seven tiles, by turn 10 — **and then sat on the site without founding a base**, turns
10 to 26, `order=0`, `built` unchanged. `enemy_move=4` over 28 turns: the executor runs, but at
the END of our turn, when the units have already spent their moves, so it almost never reaches
`mod_enemy_veh`. It is running at the wrong point in the turn.

**So the flag route does not close the ladder gate.** It travels and does not settle.

### 2. What DOES complete the cycle — and this is the useful result

`settle-mode 1` (leave en-route pods alone; let the engine's own automation walk them) with
`unit-turn 0`:

    turn 0   pod=68,92   wp=-1,-1     at_base=1
    turn 1   pod=68,92   wp=64,90
    turn 2   pod=66,92 -> 64,90        arrived
    turn 15  built 1 -> 2              FOUNDED

Produced, travelled, settled, in three turns. Reproduced on a second seeded run:
(136,144) -> (140,142) by turn 3.

**The remaining freeze is narrower than this bead's title.** It is not "pods do not travel" — a
pod in the field travels at full speed and settles. It is that a pod **standing in a base** does
not leave it. At turn 49 of the combination run: `pod=136,144 at_base=1 wp=124,146`, nine pods
queued (`build-stats queued=9`), two ever settled, bases 7:2 against AIs on 5-9.

### 3. Elimination #7, and a self-correction

thinker 5b60ed2 skipped `VSTATE_UNK_40000` for player pods on the reasoning that the flags hand
the unit to a mover that never runs. The state bits looked like they confirmed it —

    travelling pod  state=0x40000 in base, 0x70004 moving, settles
    frozen pod      state=0x10 (no 0x40000), never leaves

— so I restored the flags. With them restored the frozen pod reads `state=0x60000`, 0x40000 SET,
and is **still frozen** at (129,81) from turn 22 to 31. The bit does not separate the cases.
Reverted in **d73d5b3**, engine behaviour restored, and written down rather than quietly undone:
the same change measured against two configurations gave opposite readings, and only the second
had a pod that could move at all.

### Where this leaves the ladder

Not blocked on binary RE, and sattler's altitude check was the right call — the flag route was
worth measuring first and it changed the shape of the problem. The narrow question now is why a
pod standing IN a base does not leave, when the starting pod leaves that same base on turn 2 of
the same game. `home_base_id`, the unit design, and stacking are the untested differences, and
all three are readable from `move-stats` without touching the binary.

I told sattler the remaining freeze was "a pod IN A BASE does not leave". That was the correlate

comments.text:
na-1lj hypothesis FROM THE GAME RULES, not measurement — marked INFERRED until your counter speaks.

MECHANIC (documented SMAC behavior; our own alphax.txt line 80: CentPsi = "Technology to ease fungus movement"; Xenoempathy Dome = "Fungus Movement Bonus"): moving INTO a fungus tile pre-CentPsi consumes the unit's ENTIRE remaining movement and the entry can FAIL outright, repeatedly, until a roll succeeds.

WHY IT FITS YOUR SIGNATURE EXACTLY: full allowance spent + zero displacement (the failed entry eats the budget); intermittent (it is a per-attempt roll); non-positional and unpredicted by everything measured so far — because the predictor is the TERRAIN OF THE NEXT TILE ON THE PATH, which no instrument has looked at yet. Also explains "several still turns then a full-speed move": one successful roll and the pod sprints.

IF CONFIRMED, the fix is design not code: settle-path should avoid fungus (safe_path may already know how — check its fungus handling for AI factions), or formers clear it — and note move.cpp:1866 gates auto-former fungus removal on !is_human: potential family member #7.

comments.author: harding
comments.text:
## ROOT CAUSE FOUND — and the tooling that found it in four minutes

**A destination whose FIRST STEP the pod cannot afford.** Measured on the `frozen-pod-seed1`
fixture:

    path=16                       a VALID route — about six turns of travel
    step=134,84  dir=5  cost=6    the pathfinder's own first step
    speed=3                       the pod's entire allowance

The first stride costs **double** everything the unit has, and movement does not accumulate
across turns, so it can never be taken. The pod sat on one tile for nineteen turns holding a
perfectly valid route to a perfectly reachable site.

This is the first hypothesis that predicts EVERY earlier observation rather than part of one:

- frozen indefinitely, not slowly — the step is impossible, not expensive
- frozen under the default, under `settle-mode 1`, and with `colony_move` running twice a turn
- unrelated to fungus (`sfung=0` — it is the rocky tile), ZOC, bases, or state bits
- non-positional, because it turns on the terrain of ONE tile, which is why nothing positional
  ever correlated
- and why other pods travel normally: their first step is affordable

Nothing in the site search knows about step cost. `select_colony` scores destinations and
`safe_path` checks the route is safe and unowned; neither asks whether the unit can take the
first stride. So the search re-picks the same site forever.

## The fix — thinker 32d623c, and it is PARTIAL

Mark the site as taken (`NODE_BASE_SITE`, the mechanism `colony_move`'s own search already uses
to skip a tile) and clear the order so the pod re-plans in the same turn. `mapnodes` is cleared
each turn by `move_upkeep`, so this is a one-turn exclusion applied immediately before the
re-plan — not a permanent ban on a tile that may be reachable later from elsewhere.

In OUR pass, not in `colony_move`: the same search runs for AI factions, which have working
movement, and changing it there would alter seven factions' behaviour to fix one faction's stall.

cause as a cure.

Every one of the eleven eliminations before this cost a fresh 15-minute run that landed on a
different map position — so no two were the same experiment. Stiwi's call to use save states
changed that: `frozen-pod-seed1` reproduces the stuck pod in **59 seconds**, byte-identical, and

argument caps the total route cost, so passing the unit's speed asks "can I arrive THIS turn" —
which is -1 for any real journey. Passing it would have read as "no route exists" and closed the
bead on a false answer. Caught before it was measured, and both numbers are now reported:
`path` with a cap far above any route, `path1` with the unit's own speed.

    NA_SAVE=evals/fixtures/<name>.sav scripts/play-thinker.sh headless

title: Engine crash at 004BF423 when our HQ base is lost — kills any 250-turn ladder row
description:
Both seeded ladder attempts died at the same instruction, and the register dump is IDENTICAL
across two runs 2.5 hours and one rebuild apart:

    ExceptionCode    c0000005          (access violation, read)
    ExceptionAddress 004bf423
    EAX 00000000   EBX 00000280   ESI 0022899c   EBP 00228940   ESP 00228844

    attempt 1  thinker b36bc52  turn 122/123  2026-08-23 09:15:47
    attempt 2  thinker be1b51b  turn 126      2026-08-23 11:45:35

Byte-identical registers on two different builds is a DETERMINISTIC code path, not memory
corruption that happened to land twice.

## The trigger

Both crashes fire on dismissing the dialog that reports OUR HEADQUARTERS BASE BEING LOST.

    attempt 1   PSYCH CHAPLAIN: "Our citizens are starving at U.N. Headquarters!"
                -> the base was gone at turn 123 (7:0, faction eliminated)
    attempt 2   SECURITY CHIEF: "University seizes U.N. Headquarters! 63 energy credits
                diverted from local nets."  -> HQ captured at turn 126

Both were a 4-bar / 3-row dialog and both crashed within a second of the click that dismissed it.

## The instruction

Code at the fault, from the crash dump:

    8B 10               mov edx,[eax]        <- EAX is 0. This is the fault.
    FF 52 08            call [edx+8]         <- a vtable call on a null object
    8B 86 0C 01 00 00   mov eax,[esi+0x10C]
    89 BE 10 01 00      mov [esi+0x110],edi

A null `this` followed by a virtual call, in the unnamed function between
`TutWin_operator_delete` (0x4BEA20) and `compute_camera` (0x4BF740) — a drawing path. ESI is a
stack object (0x22899c) with members at 0x10C/0x110. Return address on the stack is 0x4bf5ad,
in the same region.

Consistent with the engine drawing something that refers to a base which no longer exists.

## NOT caused by our production fix

Attempt 1 ran on b36bc52, which predates `na_manage_player_bases` entirely. The crash is older
than anything landed today.

## Why it may matter less than it looks

Both crashes required LOSING THE HQ, which required the faction collapsing, which is
thinker 7f9693f's territory — `move_upkeep(UM_Player)` has never run for our slot, so every
expansion decision ran on a cleared map. A faction that does not collapse may never raise this
dialog. **That is a reason to re-measure, not a reason to close this**: an engine crash on a
routine game event is a hard ceiling on any 250-turn ladder row, and the next row that loses a
base for an ordinary reason hits it again.

## What would settle it

1. Does it reproduce on STOCK Thinker (no NA build)? That separates "SMAC/Thinker bug we must
   avoid triggering" from "ours".
2. Does 7f9693f's upkeep fix stop the faction collapsing far enough that the dialog never fires?

Both captured dumps have EAX=0 and identical registers, so the direct cause is a null secondary draw-surface Release call. The two final frames show the same HQ-capture notice over a normal map; this is not only the earlier stacked-base-screen condition.

comments.author: harding
comments.text:
## FIXED — thinker be1b51b. Cause was none of the four candidates, and the census is why we know.

`mod_base_reset` is **never called for a base owned by the human faction at all** — not called and
skipped, never called. Its only per-faction caller is `mod_bases_reset`, which opens with
`if (is_human(faction_id)) return;`. So Thinker's production AI never runs for our bases, the
ColonyUnit branch in `select_build_inner` is never evaluated, and nothing ever queues a colony
pod. The faction founds its starting base and stops, whatever `manage_player_bases` says.

MEASURED, one run, with a positive control (turn 10, seed 1):

    player=7 reset_enter=0 reset_managed=0 build_run=0 reached=0 queued=0
             ai_reset_enter=33 ai_build_run=12

The AI columns are the control and they matter: without them a row of zeros means either "this
never happens for us" or "this instrument never fired", and only one is a finding.

**The governor flag I would have blamed is SET** — `may_pod=1`, `gov=0xDFBF41`. Reading the
source pointed at `GOV_MAY_PROD_COLONY_POD` and at `allow_expand`; both were wrong. That is the
third time on this workstream that reading the source produced a confident wrong answer and a
counter at the call site settled it in one run (na-4zs, na-ywn, now this).

## The fix

`na_manage_player_bases()` — same seam and same shape as `na_settle_player_colonies` — runs
`mod_base_reset` over our faction's bases once per turn, AFTER the settle pass so a base founded
this turn gets its production chosen this turn. Gated on `manage_player_bases`, so it is a no-op
for a real player.

Deliberately NOT a change to `mod_bases_reset`'s early return: that return is correct for a human
playing normally — nobody wants the AI rewriting their build queue — and `manage_player_bases` is
precisely the flag that opts out of it.

## Before and after, same seed, same build

| turn | before | after | AIs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 9  | -   | **7:2** | 2 each |
| 13 | 7:1 | -       | 2 each |
| 21 | 7:1 | **7:3** | 2-3 |

`win_ladder`'s viability checkpoint went from **REFUSED** at turn 20 to **ok** on the same seed —
that is the harness's own instrument agreeing, not my reading of it.

Census after the fix: `build_run=3 reached=2 queued=2 no_gov=0 no_site=0` — the branch runs, and
queues a pod every time it is reached.

## What stays

The counters and the `build-stats` command are permanent. They are the instrument that settled
this, and they make the next expansion question answerable in one run instead of three.

comments.text:
# na-px5 DONE — seeded starts work, and the acceptance pair earned its place

thinker `7dbde20`, NA `play-thinker.sh` (`NA_SEED`). na-clk's approved seed is unblocked.

## The acceptance pair, measured on real launches

| launch | map_seed |
|---|---|
| seed 4242, run A | **4243** |
| seed 4242, run B | **4243** — same seed, same world |
| seed 9999 | **10000** — different seed, different world |

I wrote on this bead that "a seed that is accepted and ignored looks exactly like one that
works, which is the failure this must not ship with". **It was in that state four separate
times**, and each version looked correct:

| attempt | result |
|---|---|
| seed `game_srand` in `game_init` | varied run to run — startup consumes an unpredictable number of draws before the map is built |
| re-seed immediately before `mod_world_build()` | still varied — `world_generate` does not read that generator |
| write `*MapRandomSeed` directly | still varied — the engine sets it during generation |
| **pass the seed to `world_generate` itself** | **works** |

`world_generate` takes its seed as an ARGUMENT, from `next_rand()` — a **different generator**
from `game_srand`. Nothing upstream of that call can make the world reproducible, and everything
upstream of it looked like it might. The fix is one line at the point of use, after three at
plausible points that did nothing at all.

## And a fourth failure that was not about randomness

QUICK START takes the map type from saved preferences, and `map_type == 2` loads
`maps\xplanet.mp` — a **premade map**. On a machine whose prefs say that, every "seeded" launch
produced the identical world regardless of seed: 4242 and 9999 both gave map_seed 24262. A
seeded launch now forces a generated map, and does not write that choice back over the human's
preference.

This is the one I would have shipped. The RNG work was visibly unfinished; a premade map
produces a perfectly plausible game every time.

## How it works, and why it is small

QUICK START already runs faction, map and difficulty setup with no dialogs — the existing
`-na-autoload` menu hook answers `#TOPMENU` index 1. So `-na-new-game` reuses that path and adds
a seed; it does not add a second setup path. Faction, map size and difficulty come from the same
preferences quickstart already uses, which is also what keeps the fairness profile stable across
seeds — the property na-xb1 pins and `win_ladder.py` refuses without.

`game-state` now reports `map_seed`, which is what turns "did the seed take effect" into a
number rather than an eyeballed map.

## ⚠️ One thing to settle BEFORE spending the approved seed

In every seeded launch, at turn 13: `bases=1:2,2:2,3:2,4:2,5:2,6:2,7:0`. **Every AI faction has
founded two bases and ours has none.** Our colony pods are not being settled.

`manage_player_units=1` is set, so this is either that flag not covering colony pods, or the
driver ending our turn before they act. A ladder run in this state loses every seed for a reason
that has nothing to do with the brain — and it would look like a decisive result.

**Filed as na-4ke.** Cheap to settle (one seeded launch, watch faction 7's base count for ~20
turns) and it must be settled first: it is exactly the shape of the 18-bases-vs-56 problem that
made the old save unusable, and it would be measured as a loss rather than as a harness fault.

## A harness limit that belongs on this result, found while running a third arm (harding)

**Both M1 arms were driven through their in-play dialogs by `scripts/drive-unattended.py`, and
that driver can take in-game ACTIONS.**

The escape hatch that unsticks a dialog rotates through its bars when clicking visibly stops
working. On a notice or a base panel every bar is inert. On a **diplomacy** dialog they are not:
"UNIVERSITY - AMBIVALENT" offers seven options including *"Let us sign a Treaty of Friendship"*
and *"I have urgent need of energy credits"*, and the driver clicked through them while an OK sat
on the bottom row.

Two things follow, and only the second is fixed:

1. **Fixed:** rotation was keyed on the TURN, so one long stall left the driver permanently in
   rotate mode and it wandered into option lists on dialogs that bottom-right would have
   dismissed first time. It is now keyed on the dialog, so bottom-right is always tried first on
   anything new.
2. **Not fixed, and a real limit on the M1 numbers:** both arms were driven by the pre-fix rule.
   The noise is symmetric in expectation — same script, same rule, same dialog classes — but it
   is not identical and it is not controlled. A diplomatic action taken in one arm and not the
   other is a difference the fairness profile cannot see.

**How much this could matter:** the M1 gap is −2,353 energy over 40 turns, driven by 54 rush-buys
whose reasoning is in the decision records. A stray diplomacy click does not produce that
pattern. So I do not think it explains the result — but "I do not think" is the right strength of
claim, and na-clk's seeded harness is what removes the doubt rather than an argument here.

**For na-clk:** a win ladder must not click game actions to unblock itself. Either the dialogs
get intercepted properly (na-4lr / na-k43's `Popup_start`), or the driver needs a
dismiss-only rule that refuses to click a bar it cannot identify as inert.

comments.text:
# na-clk: the instrument is built. The ladder itself is blocked on a seam and gated on spend.

Two deliverables landed, one blocker named with its fix, and one decision that is Stiwi's.

## 1. Victory is observable now — thinker `694ba66`

`game-state` on the command channel, verified against a live game:

    state=0x110002 done=0 halted=0 turn=141 player=7 victory=none
    bases=1:48,2:50,3:50,4:56,5:27,6:47,7:18

Raw `GameState` bits, not a verdict: the engine sets exactly one victory flag and the ladder is
what should decide what counts, so a boolean minted in the adapter would be its opinion about a
rule that lives in `RULES_VICTORY_*`. Per-faction base counts alongside, because
`STATE_VICTORY_CONQUER` says a conquest happened and not by whom.

**Without this, a ladder could only report that a run stopped.** "The process exited", "the turn
limit was reached" and "we won" are the same observation from outside.

## 2. The scorer — NA `scripts/win_ladder.py`

`report` turns per-seed endings into win / loss / **unresolved**, and states na-xb1's acceptance
rather than reducing it to a boolean:

    arm brain: 2 win / 1 loss / 0 unresolved
      seed 1      win         turn 210   conquest victory, sole surviving faction
      seed 2      loss        turn 198   conquest victory with rivals still holding bases [2]
      seed 3      win         turn 233   conquest victory, sole surviving faction
      goal (2 of 3 seeded wins): 2 of 3 — MET

**Three outcomes, not two.** A seed with no `STATE_GAME_DONE` is `unresolved`, never a loss — an
unfinished game is not a defeat, and scoring it as one flatters whichever side timed out.

Refuses a mixed fairness profile, importing `ab_outcomes.profile_key` rather than reimplementing
it so the two tools cannot drift into disagreeing about what a comparable run is. Verified on the
real reading above plus four synthetic endings and both refusals.

## 3. ⛔ THE BLOCKER: there is no seam for starting a seeded game

`run` refuses, deliberately. Starting a new game unattended needs faction, map, difficulty and
seed chosen without dialogs, and the fork stops short of that. The pieces are all bound
symbols — `MapRandomSeed` (`engine.cpp:60`, 0x949878), `game_srand` (0x538FB0),
`mod_world_build()` and `setup_game(0)` (`game.cpp:1271-1273`) — but the path around them walks
the config dialogs (`CONF_LOOP` / `CONF_RULES` / `CONF_DIFF`). So this is a bounded feature —
a `-na-new-game <seed>` flag in the same family as `-na-autoload` — and not a research question.

**And the save we have cannot substitute.** On it our faction holds **18 bases against rivals
with 27, 47, 48, 50, 50 and 56**. That is where the save starts, not something a brain did. A
ladder run on it would measure the starting position, and the number would be quoted as if it
measured the brain. That is why `run` refuses instead of doing something plausible.

## 4. ⛔ SPEND: 3 full seeds is OVER the epic's gate — Stiwi's call

Estimated from this session's measured rate rather than guessed:

| | measured / derived |
|---|---|
| per decision | **$0.0041** (723 decisions, $2.95, M2 arm) |
| decisions per turn | ~2 x base count — 18 bases gave 18/turn |
| a full game | bases grow ~1 -> 30; average ~15 -> **~30 decisions/turn** |
| 250 turns | ~7,500 decisions -> **~$31 per seed** |
| **3 seeds** | **~$92** |

**Over the USD 50 gate, so this needs Stiwi's explicit go**, per na-xb1's spend rule. Wall clock
is the other cost: my arms ran ~1 turn/minute, so a seed is ~4 hours and a 3-seed ladder ~12.

Two ways to cut it, both changing what is measured and neither mine to choose:
- **Fewer turns per seed** — a turn cap makes seeds `unresolved` rather than losses, which the
  scorer handles honestly but which does not answer "does it win".
- **One seed first** (~$31, ~4 hours), to find out whether a full game even completes unattended
  before committing three. This is what I would recommend: the harness has never run past turn
  141, and a 250-turn run will meet dialog classes the driver has not seen.

## 5. My own prerequisite on this bead, partly discharged

I wrote that "a win ladder must not click game actions to unblock itself". The rotation bug that
caused it is fixed (rotation is keyed on the dialog, so bottom-right is always tried first), but
the driver can still in principle click an option on a dialog that refuses bottom-right. A
dismiss-only rule needs to know which bars are inert, and that is what na-4lr / na-k43's
`Popup_start` interception would provide. **Recorded as a real remaining risk for any ladder
run, not as done.**

the per-seed cost, which extrapolates a 40-turn rate to a 250-turn game.

comments.text:
RULING: seeds vs ocean — BOTH, layered, and the vet must be SYMMETRIC (sattler, 2026-08-23).

1. PIN THE MAP PARAMETERS IN THE SEAM (the na-px5 flag family): ocean coverage, size, and whatever else map_menu currently draws from the RNG becomes an explicit argument with a fixed standard value for all ladder runs. Rationale: a parameter the RNG chooses is a confound injected before turn 1; fixing it removes variance at the source and is identical for all seven factions, so it biases nothing.

2. ADD A SYMMETRIC START-VIABILITY REFUSAL TO win_ladder, beside the existing fairness refusals: after generation, score EVERY faction's start by the same cheap criterion (e.g. starting-landmass tiles above a floor / not island-stranded), and REFUSE the seed if ANY faction fails — logged and counted like the profile-mismatch refusal, never silent. Two properties are load-bearing:
   - SYMMETRIC: vetting only OUR start would bias the ladder upward (we would reject our bad luck and keep the rivals'). The same bar for all seven is a fairness property, not a cherry-pick.
   - REFUSAL, NOT CAVEAT: same argument as ab-outcomes — a caveat gets skipped by the reader who likes the number. Refused seeds are part of the published record ("N seeds drawn, M refused for start-viability, wins on the rest").

3. Do NOT hand-pick seeds by inspection, ever — draw them sequentially or from a committed list decided before generation, and let the refusal rule do the rejecting. The difference between "vetted" and "cherry-picked" is exactly whether the rule was written down before the draw.

Consistency note for na-ywn's settle gap: pods with "No Orders" on the NA slot should be driven at the NATIVE tier (a small thinker-side auto-settle for the managed human slot), per the na-nmg ruling that unit movement is mechanical — do not stand up an LLM surface to found bases.

turn 122 decides about `base_id 0` and no other — measured across all 127 worldview files, not
sampled. That base grew to population 6, starved 6 -> 5 -> 4 -> 3 over turns 119-122, and was
gone at turn 123. The six CPU factions reached 22-51 bases each.

**Not the map.** The start was normal and the base grew in place; seed 4242's open-ocean start
(na-ywn) is what a map fault looks like and this is not it. Nothing in the human slot builds a
colony pod, so there was never a pod for my settle fix (b36bc52) to move — that fix addressed
settling pods that do not exist. I was wrong about where the gap was.

CONSEQUENCE for na-xb1: a faction on one base cannot beat six CPU factions on 200+, however well
it decides. **The goal cannot be measured until the LLM faction can expand**, and no number of
seeds changes that. Recommend the 3-seed request stays deferred — drawing more seeds now buys
three more refusals, not three more results.

confidence:extracted — every number above is from the run's own files.

## Two harness defects found and fixed

**1. The dismissing button was structurally undetectable** (59981e3). The run froze at turn 119
for 205 driver cycles on a PSYCH CHAPLAIN notice. The bar detector kept only the widest run per
scanline, and only if it spanned 0.20 * WINDOW width, so a side-by-side `Don't Show As Popup` |
`OK` pair could not be represented at all — window 2560, dialog 677px, OK button 335px, floor
512px. Every click landed on a real button and every layer reported ok. The rotate-on-stuck
escape hatch was useless because it can only rotate through rows it is given.

Fixed: the floor is now a fraction of the widest bar IN THE IMAGE (the dialog's own width) and
every run inside the dialog's x-extent is kept. The "is there a dialog at all" test is still the
old window-relative one, so the no-dialog path cannot regress; bars are y-clustered so a
base-management panel 350px lower cannot contribute a fake bottom row. Both arms proved on the
captured frame: OK found at (1449,832); same image with the dialog painted out returns nothing.
Hot-swapped into the live run: one click dismissed it and the game went 119 -> 122 in 90s.

**It also caused an engine crash.** Rotation clicked `Zoom to Base Control`, opening a base
screen UNDER the modal; dismissing in that stacked state crashed terranx —
`c0000005 at 004BF423`, EAX=0, `8B 10 / FF 52 08` (null this, then a vtable call), in the unnamed
drawing function between TutWin_operator_delete and compute_camera. Wine caught it as an
unhandled page fault and its debugger is what deafened the command channel. So the driver's
"the game is gone, or a modal has deafened the channel" was right on its first branch.
The rule "a win ladder must not click game actions to unblock itself" was already on this bead;
the detector bug is what forced the driver to break it.

**2. The viability bar was never applied DURING a run** (d2226c3). `win_ladder.viability` — two
bases by turn 20, same bar for all seven factions — was built for exactly this case and only ever
ran when scoring a results file afterwards. Seed 1 was below the bar at turn 20 and played on for
another 103 turns. The driver now applies it once at the checkpoint turn and stops. Once, not
repeatedly: a check that re-ran later would start refusing seeds for losing. An unanswered
game-state probe is NOT a refusal.

I also corrected two claims in win_ladder that said a refusal means "the map, not the play" —
seed 1 measured the other cause. The reason string now reports the fact and names no cause: a
refusal that guesses wrong sends the reader to the map generator when the bug is in the build
queue. Both were mine.

## Spend

USD 0.54 spent of ~USD 31 approved. I stopped the run at turn 123 of 250 rather than play it out:
the outcome was decided and the remaining ~4.5h would have measured nothing.

comments.text:
## Brain-arm composition: expected, and it is a RATE not a gate (harding)

sattler asked whether base.production/faction.se/faction.tech never reaching the LLM is
expected. Answer: **yes, and the mechanism is in the source, not in our configuration.**

`mod_base_build` — which is where `na_decide_base_production` is called from (`base.cpp:1313`)
— has **exactly one caller in the whole fork**: `base.cpp:1094`, inside `mod_base_reset`. And
`mod_base_reset` is called from five event sites (`base.cpp:74, 628, 1120, 2966, 3059`) — a base
founded, an item completed, an HQ relocation, a capture. **It is not on the per-turn path.**

So the two surfaces have fundamentally different rates:

| surface | fires |
|---|---|
| `base.hurry` | every base, every turn — via `mod_base_upkeep` (which is why na-4zs mattered) |
| `base.production` | only when a base needs a NEW item chosen |

With 18 Peacekeeper bases and turns of ~1 minute, few items complete per turn. Measured at turn
106 in the brain arm: 79 `base.hurry`, 1 `faction.tech`, 0 `base.production`. The AI factions in
the same run show 0 `base.production` too — correctly, since they are not `llm_enabled` in this
arm and that surface only records when it routes.

**Nothing is misconfigured.** `manage_player_bases=1` is set and is working: the human's bases
are being processed (170 `base.workers` and 72 `base.defend_goal` records for faction 7 in the
same window), which is what that flag buys.

### What that means for the analysis, stated plainly

**As it stands, `ab-outcomes` on this arm will be measuring the hurry policy.** sattler's framing
is right and it is worth having on the record before the numbers exist rather than after.

That is not a wasted measurement — base.hurry is the surface na-6db was FILED about ("the brain
disagreed with the deterministic tier... whether it was RIGHT is unknown"), and the na-qu8 eval
measured 0/20 agreement with Thinker on exactly this surface in both arms. So a 30-turn
outcome comparison on hurry answers the original question. It just must not be reported as "the
brain played the faction".

### The check that decides whether it stays hurry-only

`base.production` at 0 is expected at turn 106 and would NOT be expected at turn 131. If the
count is still zero at the 30-turn bar, the rate explanation is wrong and something does gate
it — so I am tracking the count per turn rather than assuming. If it stays zero I will say so
and the result gets labelled hurry-only explicitly.

If more surface coverage is wanted in a later arm, the lever is not configuration: it is running
long enough for items to complete, or seeding a save where many bases are mid-build.

projection that production decisions accumulate over 30 turns.
